**00:07:56–00:08:01** done, but it helps you keep your staff to what really matters, which is your competition cycle.
**00:08:01–00:08:06** The last bit really is making sure, as we've talked about previously in the course,
**00:08:06–00:08:12** know yourself and know your people. Really look at where everybody sits. Our
**00:08:12–00:08:18** discipline will fall apart when we have a difference, particularly in technology. It'll fall apart when
**00:08:18–00:08:25** our knowledge and behaviours don't match, when people don't know what they're doing, or under
**00:08:25–00:08:29** pressure, they choose not to do it, or they're lazy. You've got to stick with that. We can't
**00:08:29–00:08:34** go into a position where we have egos running things. There's people who want to own a process.
**00:08:34–00:08:40** There's also people who want to be right. We need to make sure we stay on board and aligned.
**00:08:40–00:08:43** If we know where our people are at, we can work on improving them.
**00:08:45–00:08:51** Understand that a false promise on the ground looks like this when you hear this sort of thing.
**00:08:51–00:08:56** We bought the system, so now we have objective truth. You don't. Dashboard stays red,
**00:08:56–00:09:00** so we pull someone out. If you're going to be doing that, it's not the computer's job
**00:09:00–00:09:06** to answer. The computer is just using a repeatable measure to get what you could calculate out,
**00:09:06–00:09:11** so making sure you have that stuff checked off. One of the other ones I love is we monitor
**00:09:11–00:09:15** everything all the time. The reality for many people are doing that, they've got no idea what
**00:09:15–00:09:19** they're looking at, and they're just collecting data. I've seen that plenty of times in recent
**00:09:19–00:09:25** times. To wrap up, three rules, strict rules. Standardise your data capture before you start
**00:09:25–00:09:30** scaling collection. Define what real change is and reliability within your environment,
**00:09:30–00:09:36** and make decisions the product. The product is what you do with the data, not the equipment
**00:09:36–00:09:42** themselves. Remember, the tool is not the upgrade, the discipline is. Stick with that and you'll be
**00:09:42–00:09:51** fun. Best of luck.
=== PAGE 1 ===
© SpeedSig 2025 
The False Promise of Technology without Discipline 
Buying technology in a sports performance environment often comes with an unspoken expectation: 
collect more data and performance will improve. In practice, Jason Weber argues the opposite happens 
when discipline is missing—more data becomes more noise, more arguments, and less trust. This isn’t an 
anti-technology stance. As the creator of SpeedSig, he’s clear that tools can help, but only when they’re 
operated inside a disciplined system. 
Discipline is what makes tools useful 
In simple terms, discipline means repeatable behaviour. For technology, that starts with standardised 
protocols, followed by getting the maths/statistics right, and then building consistent operations on top of 
those foundations. If any of these are missing, the tool risks becoming a “random number generator,” 
where one-oƯ measures are used to make conﬁdent claims about athletes that can’t be supported. 
Three common technology failure modes 
Weber describes three patterns that show up repeatedly in real departments: 
1. Protocol drift: The test name stays the same, but the warm-up, setup, or execution changes—
sometimes by only a small amount. Those changes can meaningfully alter outcomes, and 
leaders then struggle to trust results when they aren’t present at every test. 
2. Maths/statistics-free interpretation: People declare improvement or decline without 
understanding what change means relative to the known accuracy and reliability of the system. 
3. Communication chaos: Dashboards and data exist, but decisions are ad hoc. Key decision-
makers don’t have aligned information, actions aren’t assigned clearly, and confusion becomes 
the norm. 
A tool can’t operate your system for you 
SpeedSig is used as an example. It can describe running mechanics and speed-related signals, but it 
can’t make decisions, and it can’t automatically integrate its information with other domains (like force 
plate data) across the strength-to-running continuum. The tool must ﬁt within an operating system—
otherwise it becomes another source of debate rather than clarity. 
Three disciplines to close the gap 
Weber outlines three practical disciplines that turn technology into something useful: 
1) Protocol: “Earn the right to compare.” 
If you can’t repeat it, you can’t learn from it. Lock down what the test is and also deﬁne what it isn’t so 
you don’t overstep what the data can legitimately tell you. Establish what counts as a valid rep, what 
should be excluded, and standardise instructions and steps. This protects staƯ, supports 
onboarding, and protects athletes from false conclusions. 
2) The critical maths: don’t confuse noise for change. 
Every signal contains information and noise. You need to understand system reliability—including 
what variability to expect in your environment, potentially across diƯerent testers. Concepts like ICC 
and standard error of measurement are referenced as ways to quantify reliability and set thresholds 
for meaningful change. If you can’t explain why you trust the change, you can’t reasonably ask others 
to act on it. 
3) Communication alignment: tools don’t create alignment—leadership does. 
Discipline gives freedom: once operations are reliable, teams can be creative without losing control. 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© SpeedSig 2025 
Alignment requires shared language and shared procedures, supported by consistent meeting 
structures that create weekly “tempo” and checkpoints tied to the competition cycle. 
Know yourself and know your people 
Weber ﬁnishes by returning to leadership: departments fall apart when knowledge and behaviour don’t 
match—when people don’t know what they’re doing, don’t do it under pressure, or let ego drive the 
process. The “false promise” shows up in statements like: “We bought the system, so now we have 
objective truth,” or “The dashboard says red, so we pulled someone out,” or “We monitor everything all 
the time,” even when staƯ don’t truly understand what they’re looking at. 
The wrap: three rules 
The closing message is simple and strict: 
1. Standardise data capture before you scale collection. 
2. Deﬁne real change by understanding reliability in your environment. 
3. Make decisions the product—the product is what you do with the data, not the equipment. 
The tool is not the upgrade—discipline is.

######## Lab_2b_Capability_and_Workflow_Audit
=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Module 2 – Lab 2B:  
Capability & Workﬂow Audit 
The matrix that turns technology into decisions 
Lab 2B is simple in concept, but powerful in practice: 
What equipment do we have, what can it do, and what can it not do? 
And just as important: how does it move through our team to produce decisions? 
In small environments—one S&C coach, one physio, maybe a doctor—alignment happens naturally. 
People talk constantly, and the workﬂow is often implicit. 
But as environments grow, the risk changes: 
 
more staƯ 
 
more tools 
 
more handoƯs 
 
more opportunities for drift 
In larger systems, alignment must be designed, not hoped for. 
That’s what this audit is. 
Capability vs workﬂow (don’t confuse them) 
Capability audit 
This is the “tool truth”: 
 
What does it measure? 
 
What does it not measure? 
 
What is it useful for, and where does it become inference? 
Workﬂow audit 
This is where most departments fail. 
Workﬂow is: 
 
who captures the data 
 
how it is processed (vendor, in-house code, SpeedSig, dashboards) 
 
who interprets it 
 
how it is communicated 
 
where the decision gets made 
A device doesn’t create impact. A workﬂow does. 
Strategy vs tactic: a useful mental model 
Think of strategy as the highway: 
 
your direction 
 
your standards 
 
the key questions you care about 
Tactics are changing lanes: 
 
the day-to-day choices staƯ make 
 
which tool to deploy 
 
how to adjust tests, timing, and exposure 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
 
how to respond to what you see 
The goal is to give staƯ tactical freedom while maintaining strategic alignment. 
And the simplest tool to achieve that is a matrix. 
The Capability & Workﬂow Matrix (how to build it) 
Step 1: list your technologies (rows) 
Down the left side, list everything: 
 
computer + software stack 
 
GPS/IMU 
 
force plates 
 
load cells / force transducers 
 
linear transducers 
 
video tools 
 
wellness / subjective measures 
 
anything else relevant 
Step 2: deﬁne your applications (columns) 
Across the top, pick a structure that matches your world. 
You can deﬁne columns by: 
Option A — domains 
 
Rehab 
 
Performance 
 
Return-to-play 
 
Monitoring 
Option B — questions 
 
Hamstring injury 
 
Calf injury 
 
Adductor/groin injury 
 
Speed development 
 
Maximum strength 
 
Deceleration ability 
 
Fatigue monitoring 
Step 3: ﬁll each cell with four items 
For each technology × application, write: 
1. Purpose: what question it answers 
2. Output: the metric/report you deliver 
3. Owner: who is responsible 
4. Workﬂow: capture → process → interpret → communicate → decision 
This is where it becomes operational, not theoretical. 
A practical example (what “workﬂow” looks like) 
Hamstring rehab (triangulation workﬂow) 
 
Force transducer / dynamometry: strength capacity trend 
 
GPS/IMU: exposure dose (high-speed work, accelerations) 
 
Mechanics check (where available): strategy changes vs baseline 
 
Response checks: immediate + 24h stability 
Workﬂow includes: 
=== PAGE 3 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
 
who runs the test 
 
where the data lives 
 
who processes it 
 
how it is reported 
 
who makes the progression decision 
Deceleration capacity (performance workﬂow) 
 
GPS/IMU captures high-intensity deceleration events 
 
data may require processing (Python/R/SpeedSig) 
 
output becomes a trend report + exposure tolerance summary 
 
decision becomes programming adjustments (load, density, drill selection) 
Notice: the value isn’t the tool. 
The value is that the tool is embedded in a repeatable, communicable decision pathway. 
Why this matters for leadership (and your career) 
A capability and workﬂow audit becomes a leadership asset: 
 
For staƯ: clarity, onboarding, and alignment 
 
For departments: discipline in process, freedom in execution 
 
For budgets: a clean argument for what is missing and why 
 
For performance review: documented procedures and decision systems are high value 
Technologies will change over time, but not overnight. 
This matrix is repeatable. It travels with you across clubs and contexts. 
And in high-performance sport, where chaos is always trying to creep in, the ability to create structure is 
one of the most valuable skills you can demonstrate. 
Lab task: what to submit for Lab 2B 
1. A one-page Capability & Workﬂow Matrix (rows = tech, columns = applications) 
2. For at least 10 “cells”, complete: 
o 
purpose 
o 
output 
o 
owner 
o 
workﬂow steps 
3. Identify: 
o 
gaps (what you can’t currently answer) 
o 
bottlenecks (where workﬂow breaks) 
o 
handoƯ risks (where communication fails) 
######## Lab_2c_Monitoring_or_Testing
=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Module 2 – Lab 2C:  
Monitoring vs Testing 
Two purposes, two-time horizons—don’t mash them together 
Monitoring and testing are both valuable. But they are not the same thing. 
And when we confuse them—when we mash them together—the eƯectiveness of both gets lost. 
This lab gives you a clean separation and a procedure you can walk into any environment with. 
Monitoring: short-term observation to guide near-term decisions 
Monitoring is short-term. 
It’s the ongoing pulse check that helps you answer: 
“Has something changed right now?” 
Monitoring typically sits on a horizon of days to weeks, where the goal is not to prove long-term 
improvement, but to detect meaningful deviations from an athlete’s usual level. 
Examples of monitoring outputs: 
 
day-to-day jump performance 
 
session exposure and tolerance (e.g., high-speed running dose) 
 
readiness markers (subjective or objective) 
 
short-term fatigue signals 
Monitoring is most valuable when it directly informs: 
 
load adjustments 
 
recovery decisions 
 
progression or regression of exposure 
 
short-term risk management 
Monitoring is status and trend. 
Testing: longer-term evaluation of capacity change 
Testing is longer reach. 
It answers a diƯerent question: 
“Have we improved capacity across a training phase?” 
Testing sits on a horizon of weeks to months. It is how you evaluate adaptation: 
 
pre-season start vs pre-season end 
 
block one vs block two 
 
year one vs year ﬁve 
Testing tells you whether the program is working, whether key capacities are developing, and whether an 
athlete is moving toward return-to-performance benchmarks. 
Testing is progress. 
Don’t misuse the methods: short-term tools aren’t seasonal tools 
A common mistake is taking short-term monitoring methods—like rolling averages or exponentially 
weighted moving averages—and treating them like long-term evaluation tools. 
Those methods are excellent for answering: 
 
“Is the athlete drifting from baseline this week?” 
But they are not designed to answer: 
 
“Did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase?” 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs post, block 
vs block), not just continuous smoothing. 
You don’t need to become a statistician here. The rule is simpler: 
DiƯerent questions require diƯerent analysis. 
The procedure rule that keeps you honest 
This is the core operating principle: 
Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then 
choose the technology. 
Too often we do it backwards: 
 
“We have force plates—so we should jump.” 
 
“We have GPS—so we should report something.” 
That’s technology-led practice, and it creates noise. 
Quality-led practice asks: 
 
What capacity matters for this sport, this coach, this phase, this athlete? 
 
Are we monitoring it (short-term decisions) or testing it (phase change)? 
 
When is it scheduled inside the periodised plan? 
Monitoring and testing should not be random. They should be planned. 
Coaches don’t need more numbers. They need clarity. 
When you work with a new coach or a new staƯ group, the winning move is simple communication: 
 
What are we evaluating? 
 
Why are we evaluating it? 
 
How often will we do it? 
 
What will you receive as output? 
 
What will we do if it changes? 
That’s the trade. 
“For this time commitment, here’s what you get back.” 
The missing link: a decision matrix 
Data becomes valuable when it triggers action. 
A simple decision matrix looks like this: 
If we get this result → we do these steps → owned by these people → reviewed at this time point. 
Example (hamstring context): 
 
If eccentric knee ﬂexor force drops meaningfully: 
o 
conﬁrm test quality / re-test 
o 
physio screen + ROM checks as indicated 
o 
adjust exposure plan 
o 
reassess response immediately and at 24 hours 
o 
progress only when stable 
That structure: 
 
aligns staƯ 
 
manages coach expectations 
 
prevents overreaction to single data points 
 
turns “numbers” into workﬂow 
=== PAGE 3 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Apply it to scenarios (why this matters in rehab) 
When a clear scenario exists—say an 8-week ankle injury—your monitoring/testing protocol becomes 
straightforward: 
 
these are the capacities we need 
 
these are the tests we will use 
 
this is the monitoring frequency 
 
this is the technology we’ll deploy 
 
this is how results connect to return-to-run and progression decisions 
With that in place, a department can be built around repeatable decision-making—not random data 
capture. 
Lab task: what to submit for Lab 2C 
1. Write your deﬁnitions: 
 
Monitoring = __________ 
 
Testing = __________ 
2. Choose one quality (e.g., deceleration capacity, jump performance, hamstring capacity)

Monitoring vs Testing 
Two purposes, two-time horizons—don’t mash them together 
Monitoring and testing are both valuable. But they are not the same thing. 
And when we confuse them—when we mash them together—the eƯectiveness of both gets lost. 
This lab gives you a clean separation and a procedure you can walk into any environment with. 
Monitoring: short-term observation to guide near-term decisions 
Monitoring is short-term. 
It’s the ongoing pulse check that helps you answer: 
“Has something changed right now?” 
Monitoring typically sits on a horizon of days to weeks, where the goal is not to prove long-term 
improvement, but to detect meaningful deviations from an athlete’s usual level. 
Examples of monitoring outputs: 
 
day-to-day jump performance 
 
session exposure and tolerance (e.g., high-speed running dose) 
 
readiness markers (subjective or objective) 
 
short-term fatigue signals 
Monitoring is most valuable when it directly informs: 
 
load adjustments 
 
recovery decisions 
 
progression or regression of exposure 
 
short-term risk management 
Monitoring is status and trend. 
Testing: longer-term evaluation of capacity change 
Testing is longer reach. 
It answers a diƯerent question: 
“Have we improved capacity across a training phase?” 
Testing sits on a horizon of weeks to months. It is how you evaluate adaptation: 
 
pre-season start vs pre-season end 
 
block one vs block two 
 
year one vs year ﬁve 
Testing tells you whether the program is working, whether key capacities are developing, and whether an 
athlete is moving toward return-to-performance benchmarks. 
Testing is progress. 
Don’t misuse the methods: short-term tools aren’t seasonal tools 
A common mistake is taking short-term monitoring methods—like rolling averages or exponentially 
weighted moving averages—and treating them like long-term evaluation tools. 
Those methods are excellent for answering: 
 
“Is the athlete drifting from baseline this week?” 
But they are not designed to answer: 
 
“Did the athlete improve meaningfully across a training phase?” 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Long-term change needs comparisons that respect time blocks and phase structure (pre vs post, block 
vs block), not just continuous smoothing.

DiƯerent questions require diƯerent analysis.

Start with the quality you want to evaluate. Then decide whether you are monitoring or testing. Then 
choose the technology.

 
“We have force plates—so we should jump.” 
 
“We have GPS—so we should report something.”



 
Are we monitoring it (short-term decisions) or testing it (phase change)? 


Monitoring and testing should not be random. They should be planned. 
Coaches don’t need more numbers. They need clarity. 
When you work with a new coach or a new staƯ group, the winning move is simple communication: 


 
Why are we evaluating it? 
 
How often will we do it? 




######## Lab_2D_Decision_Gates
=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Module 2 – Lab 2D:  
Designing Decision Gates 
The structure that turns data into decisions 
Technology gives you numbers. Numbers don’t automatically create clarity. 
In high-performance and rehab environments, what creates clarity is structure—a repeatable system 
that tells everyone: 
 
what we’re evaluating 
 
what standards matter 
 
who decides 
 
and what happens next 
That structure is a decision gate. 
What is a decision gate? 
A decision gate is a predeﬁned checkpoint in your workﬂow where you review agreed criteria and make 
a clear call before progressing: 
Go / Modify / Stop 
Decision gates stop departments from “dumping data” on coaches and senior medical staƯ and hoping 
people interpret it the same way. 
They replace randomness with a shared operating system. 
The ﬁve parts of a strong decision gate 
1) What’s being evaluated (the key quality) 
This is the most common failure point: being too vague. 
Don’t say: 
 
“hamstring injury” 
 
“hamstring capacity” 
Be speciﬁc about what capacity and what contraction/task you are assessing, for example: 
 
eccentric knee ﬂexor strength 
 
isometric hip extension strength 
 
sprint exposure tolerance (deﬁned speed band and volume) 
 
deceleration exposure tolerance (deﬁned intensity and count) 
If you can’t name it precisely, you can’t build a gate around it. 
2) Criteria (thresholds or standards) 
Criteria must be agreed in advance and written clearly. 
A practical way to write criteria is: 
 
Pass criteria (green): proceed 
 
Fail criteria (red): stop/regress 
 
Borderline (amber): conﬁrm, repeat, or add another data point 
Also deﬁne what counts as a “breach.” Otherwise, people argue after the fact. 
3) The decision options 
At a gate, you don’t just “review.” You decide. 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Common options: 
 
Progress 
 
Hold 
 
Regress 
 
Refer (e.g., to medical lead) 
 
Escalate (e.g., specialist imaging or surgical opinion) 
The option list should reﬂect the realities of your sport and medical setup. 
4) Ownership (who makes the call) 
This matters more than most people realise. 
Decision gates work when it’s clear who: 
 
provides inputs 
 
interprets results 
 
and owns the ﬁnal call 
In many systems, performance staƯ and medical staƯ share inputs, but a speciﬁc role owns the decision 
(especially in return-to-play progression). 
If ownership is unclear, gates become meetings instead of decisions. 
5) Next step (what happens after the decision) 
A gate without a next step is just conversation. 
Every gate should trigger immediate action, for example: 
 
If pass → progress to the next exposure stage 
 
If fail → regress and re-test in 72 hours 
 
If borderline → repeat test + add another measure (and set the review time) 
This turns the gate into an operational workﬂow. 
Why decision gates reduce confusion 
When staƯ send random reports to coaches and senior medical personnel, confusion is almost 
guaranteed. People interpret numbers diƯerently, and emotion enters the room—especially around 
selection. 
Decision gates prevent that because the rules are agreed before the pressure arrives. 
They create: 
 
structure 
 
conﬁdence 
 
predictable workﬂows 
 
clearer communication 
 
faster decision-making 
Build timeframes into the gate (logistics matter) 
Decision gates should also include expected timeframes. 
An athlete gets injured in a game: what happens next depends on the sport’s reality. 
Some environments can access imaging immediately. Many cannot. 
So you set expectations early: 
 
“First clinical review happens within X hours.” 
 
“Imaging is expected within Y days if criteria are met.” 
 
“First progression gate occurs on Day Z, assuming symptoms and function allow.” 
That protects trust with coaches because you’re not improvising timelines after the injury occurs. 
=== PAGE 3 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026

Create two decision gates: 
1. Performance gate (e.g., speed exposure progression or deceleration capacity) 
2. Rehab gate (e.g., hamstring return-to-run) 
For each gate, write: 
 
key quality (speciﬁc) 
 
criteria (pass/fail/borderline) 
 
decision options 
 
ownership 
 
next step + timeframe 
######## Lab_2E_The_Critcal_Math_that_can_t_be_Ignored
=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Module 2 Lab 2E:  
The Critical Math That Cannot Be Ignored 
Why reliability, error, and thresholds sit underneath every decision gate 
Technology doesn’t become valuable because it measures something. 
It becomes valuable when you can answer one question with conﬁdence: 
Is this change real—or is it noise? 
If you skip the maths, you can still collect data. 
But you cannot interpret it responsibly, and you cannot build decision gates that hold up under pressure. 
This lab outlines the minimum statistical thinking you need to use technology properly in performance 
and rehab. 
Two critical paths: system reliability and individual sensitivity 
1) System-level reliability (can we trust the test at all?) 
Reliability is not just the device. It’s the entire system: 
 
the equipment 
 
the protocol 
 
the tester 
 
the environment 
 
the athlete’s execution 
At the system level, you need to know: 
 
Intraclass correlation coeƯicient (ICC): how consistently athletes are ranked across repeated 
trials (relative reliability) 
 
Standard error of measurement (SEM) / typical error (TE): the size of the noise in the units you 
care about (absolute reliability) 
 
Minimal detectable change (MDC95): how much change is required to be conﬁdent the shift is 
beyond typical measurement noise at a high conﬁdence level 
In plain language: 
SEM/TE tells you how noisy the test is. MDC95 tells you how much change you need before you can 
call it “real.” 
2) Individual-level monitoring sensitivity (can we detect meaningful change in this athlete?) 
Monitoring is personal. Athletes have diƯerent levels of variability. 
For individual monitoring, you should understand the athlete’s typical ﬂuctuation using: 
 
Typical error / within-athlete variability 
 
Often summarised as coeƯicient of variation (CV%) for repeated measures 
That variability helps you deﬁne: 
 
Smallest worthwhile change (SWC): the smallest change that is practically meaningful—not 
just statistically real 
This is the key distinction: 
 
MDC answers: “Is it beyond noise?” 
 
SWC answers: “Is it worth caring about?” 
Both matter, but they serve diƯerent purposes. 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Why this matters: decision gates require thresholds 
Decision gates only work when thresholds are set in advance. 
And thresholds are impossible to defend if you don’t know: 
 
how noisy the measurement is 
 
how much change is required to be conﬁdent it’s real 
 
what magnitude of change is meaningful for decision-making 
A practical way to think about it: 
 
If change is below MDC95 → likely noise 
 
If change is above MDC95 → likely real 
 
If change is above SWC → likely meaningful 
 
If change is above both → you can act conﬁdently 
 
If change is real but not meaningful → note it, watch it, but don’t overreact 
That logic is what turns a data point into a decision pathway. 
Not all metrics are created equal (RFD is a classic example) 
Some metrics are inherently noisier than others. 
A great example is rate of force development (RFD). In many environments it shows higher variability 
because: 
 
execution consistency matters enormously 
 
onset detection choices matter 
 
small timing diƯerences create large changes in calculated RFD 
The takeaway is not “never use RFD.” 
The takeaway is: 
When a metric is noisy, your thresholds must be wider, your protocol must be tighter, or you choose 
a more stable metric for decision gates. 
The leadership angle: rigour creates trust 
From a high-performance management perspective, this is non-negotiable. 
If staƯ are using tests with unknown reliability, then when they bring you a number—there is no 
foundation for trust. 
Statistical rigour gives you: 
 
credibility 
 
consistent reporting 
 
defensible thresholds 
 
decision gates that work 
And in high-performance sport, where decisions are scrutinised, that’s the diƯerence between “data” and 
leadership. 
=== PAGE 3 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Lab task: what to submit for Lab 2E 
1. List your top 5 tests/metrics and for each include: 
 
ICC (if available) 
 
SEM/TE (absolute error) 
 
MDC95 (or your chosen decision threshold) 
2. For one key monitoring metric, estimate: 
 
within-athlete variability (TE or CV%) 
 
SWC (your “worth acting on” threshold) 
3. Write one decision gate statement using your thresholds: 
 
“If change is > ___, we do ___; if not, we ___.”

A practical way to think about it: 
 
If change is below MDC95 → likely noise 
 
If change is above MDC95 → likely real 
 
If change is above SWC → likely meaningful 
 
If change is above both → you can act conﬁdently 
 
If change is real but not meaningful → note it, watch it, but don’t overreact 
That logic is what turns a data point into a decision pathway. 
Not all metrics are created equal (RFD is a classic example) 
Some metrics are inherently noisier than others. 
A great example is rate of force development (RFD). In many environments it shows higher variability 
because: 
 
execution consistency matters enormously 
 
onset detection choices matter 
 
small timing diƯerences create large changes in calculated RFD 
The takeaway is not “never use RFD.” 
The takeaway is: 
When a metric is noisy, your thresholds must be wider, your protocol must be tighter, or you choose 
a more stable metric for decision gates. 
The leadership angle: rigour creates trust 
From a high-performance management perspective, this is non-negotiable. 
If staƯ are using tests with unknown reliability, then when they bring you a number—there is no 
foundation for trust. 
Statistical rigour gives you: 
 
credibility 
 
consistent reporting 
 
defensible thresholds 
 
decision gates that work 
And in high-performance sport, where decisions are scrutinised, that’s the diƯerence between “data” and 
leadership.

**00:00:40–00:00:45** to go up into leadership, you need to understand this because you need to set up your environment
**00:00:45–00:00:50** to handle this. And if you can't do this type of analysis, you need staff that can. So this
**00:00:50–00:00:56** is the critical math that can't be ignored. So technology provides one thing, measurement.
**00:00:56–00:01:02** But it's your system that provides the critical interpretation. Measuring things is easy, but
**00:01:02–00:01:06** interpreting is the hard part. If you can't separate signal from noise, then you can't
**00:01:06–00:01:11** make defensible decisions. So we need to go through this math. So there are two paths
**00:01:11–00:01:17** we need to follow here. We need to go down path one, which is system level reliability.
**00:01:17–00:01:22** Can we trust this test at all? Now, reliability in this sense means we're evaluating the
**00:01:22–00:01:27** whole system. The equipment, the protocol, the tester, the environment, the whole thing.
**00:01:27–00:01:32** So the metrics we need to know. I see it's the inter-class correlation, which gives us
**00:01:32–00:01:37** relative reliability. SCMs, the standard error of measurement or typical error, gives us
**00:01:37–00:01:42** absoluteness. And then minimal detectable change, typically in the nofop remote range,
**00:01:42–00:01:46** which gives us change required to be confident that it's real. Understanding that about
**00:01:46–00:01:51** our system gives us a knowledge about the tests in and of itself. Then we need to know
**00:01:51–00:01:57** about path two, which is the individual level monitoring sensitivity. So can we
**00:01:57–00:02:02** detect meaningful change for this athlete? So knowing what their typical
**00:02:02–00:02:08** variability is. So typical error to the within athlete, standard deviation and
**00:02:08–00:02:13** coefficient of variance. But we also need smallest, worthwhile change. So we need
**00:02:13–00:02:18** to be able to say they're two different purposes. We want to know what's real
**00:02:18–00:02:22** and what's worth caring about. So NDC will fundamentally tell you what's beyond
**00:02:22–00:02:27** noise or smaller, smaller, worthwhile change to what's worth acting on. So why
**00:02:27–00:02:31** do these decisions matter for thresholds and decision gates? We can't have a
**00:02:31–00:02:35** decision. If we're measuring, we can't make a valid decision unless we understand
**00:02:35–00:02:39** the difference in the sequence of what's changed. Thresholds are going to require
**00:02:39–00:02:42** error estimates. So we need to know where the gaps are. So without
**00:02:42–00:02:46** standard error and typical error and minimal detectable change in small
**00:02:46–00:02:51** intervals worthwhile, you can't predefine pass-fail criteria. And you need that
**00:02:51–00:02:56** before you go in. Because if we start testing and going, oh, okay, it's a little
**00:02:56–00:03:00** bit different. Well, no, it's okay. We'll let this player go. Well, no, then your
**00:03:00–00:03:05** system starts to follow. I mean, it's viable for us to have something that
**00:03:05–00:03:09** falls outside of a range, but a coach might want to take a risk. Then our
**00:03:09–00:03:16** probability of re-injury or lack of performance goes up. So we can convey
**00:03:16–00:03:22** that. Coach, this has fallen outside of our scope. This athlete is actually worse
**00:03:22–00:03:26** than they were last week. Your decision is, do they need to play or not? But
**00:03:26–00:03:30** they're going in in a lower capability. That's the discussion that typically go
**00:03:30–00:03:34** on. But you need to give them an example. A simple script examples would be,
**00:03:34–00:03:40** if the change is greater than minimal detectable change, then it's likely real.
**00:03:40–00:03:44** If the change is greater than smallest worthwhile, it's likely meaningful to
**00:03:44–00:03:48** the individual. If they're both, you can act with confidence. If they're neither,
**00:03:48–00:03:53** it's likely any difference is just noise. Now, the practical reality of this
**00:03:53–00:03:58** is that some tests are really noisy. In my opinion, tests around RFD tend to be
**00:03:58–00:04:03** more noisy. So if RFD is a highly variable signal, because of its
**00:04:03–00:04:08** execution and analysis, then analysis choices really matter. So what I don't
**00:04:08–00:04:13** like is in my environment, when I have a physiotherapist come rushing you to my
**00:04:13–00:04:18** office and say, hey, this athlete's RFD is off by 12%. And it's like, hang on,
**00:04:18–00:04:24** that's well inside our range of variability with the MDC. So it's not
**00:04:24–00:04:29** anything we can detect as real change. It's important to have those things set
**00:04:29–00:04:33** up. So when we know the variability is high, we can widen our thresholds and
**00:04:33–00:04:40** improve the protocol or we can choose a more stable metric. For leadership,
**00:04:40–00:04:44** payoff here is trust, efficiency, defensible decision. If the staff use
**00:04:44–00:04:48** tests with unknown reliability, you can't trust the data they bring you. So
**00:04:48–00:04:52** statistics will create rigor that creates trust in metrics. And this
**00:04:52–00:04:57** trust underpins our decision gates and our department credibility. So if you
**00:04:57–00:05:01** can't quantify noise, you can't defend your decisions. Good luck.

Based on the locally generated transcript of the video. Times refer to the MP4; the machine transcript is unverified. This summarizes the speaker’s framework rather than validating the examples.
The speaker argues that technology should support a training or rehabilitation question, not determine the question. A measurement is what a tool actually captures, such as force, distance, speed, or displacement. An inference is the explanation applied to that output, such as fatigue, tissue status, or readiness. (00:00–01:45)
His examples are a lower countermovement-jump result being called “neurological fatigue” and a GPS change being called “tissue stress.” Neither label follows directly from the measurement alone. Athletes can also produce a similar output through different movement strategies, so a stable score may hide a change in mechanics. (01:45–03:20)
The proposed approach is to combine several relevant observations and state the conclusion with appropriate uncertainty. In the hamstring example, the speaker mentions injury context, strength tests at different positions, jumping and hopping, speed exposure, and running mechanics. One test returning to baseline is treated as one data point rather than a stand-alone clearance. These examples are illustrative, not validated clearance criteria. (03:20–05:02)
The practical communication rule is: **report what was measured, identify what is inferred, express confidence in that inference, and recommend the next exposure or check.** (05:02–06:02)
**00:00:20–00:00:25** looking at measurement versus inference and how to communicate it. Why is this not obvious?
**00:00:25–00:00:30** All of us have worked in tech-rich environments pretty much since day one. Technology becomes
**00:00:30–00:00:35** invisible. It's kind of like your phone or furniture. That's why we need to define its
**00:00:35–00:00:39** role properly. Here's the definition that keeps you sane. Author Jim Collins wrote a book called
**00:00:39–00:00:46** Good to Great. In that book, which was based on the high performance of Fortune 500 companies,
**00:00:46–00:00:52** he said very, very clearly, technology is an accelerator. It's not a creator of momentum.
**00:00:52–00:00:57** That's what we need to make sure we focus on. Technology supports good practice. It doesn't
**00:00:57–00:01:03** replace it. So our practice in strength and conditioning sport science is science and the
**00:01:03–00:01:09** adaption at progressive training exposure. We use tools to measure that progression or the progression
**00:01:09–00:01:14** of that ideal. We don't adapt the ideal to suit the tool. Now comes the trap. Confusing
**00:01:14–00:01:19** measurement with knowing. Measurement versus inference. You've got to make a distinction.
**00:01:19–00:01:26** Measurement is what the tool captures for time, distance, speed, displacement. But inference
**00:01:26–00:01:31** is what you think it means about tissue, fatigue, readiness. Understanding that those
**00:01:31–00:01:38** measurements of force, they infer a change in the tissue. We don't know. But saying to someone
**00:01:38–00:01:45** that the tissue has changed is absolutely ludicrous. Two quick examples. Force plate. We get a change
**00:01:46–00:01:51** in counter movement jump. Performance drops. We call that neurological fatigue. We have no idea.
**00:01:51–00:01:57** We're not measuring specifically the synapses, the electrical signal out of the brain. We don't know
**00:01:57–00:02:04** that there's a central fatigue there. We've seen or identified a drop in performance. That's it.
**00:02:04–00:02:09** Same with GPS. We get a distance or a speed change measured. Somehow we say that's inferred
**00:02:09–00:02:17** tissue stress. We don't know. Coaches go nuts, certainly smart ones, when we oversell inference
**00:02:17–00:02:23** with certainty. Fundamentally, humans make it worse because humans are adaptable and redundant
**00:02:23–00:02:30** systems. They can create the same output using different strategies. Humans solve problems.
**00:02:31–00:02:37** Simple as that, and athletes solve problems. The same score can hide a different mechanic.
**00:02:37–00:02:41** The what may remain the same, but the how changes significantly, which, to be honest,
**00:02:41–00:02:47** is the core construct of speed speed. We're trying to understand, has movement mechanics
**00:02:47–00:02:53** changed even though velocity may remain the same? That can occur, but we need to understand
**00:02:53–00:02:59** if the how's changing. Think of it. We look at other elements of sport as proxy metrics,
**00:02:59–00:03:04** particularly in swimming. I grew up in swimming, and we look at swimming stroke count.
**00:03:04–00:03:10** Swimming stroke count over distance and speed gives us an idea of exactly what the person's
**00:03:10–00:03:14** doing, but you go to fields sport, it's a lot noisier because we have absolute distance,
**00:03:14–00:03:19** but we don't know what it costs per step to do that. What do we need to do?
**00:03:20–00:03:26** We need to triangulate. Triangulate, if you understand your GPS, which I hope people do,
**00:03:26–00:03:32** is about using multiple sources to establish where something is in space. We want to build
**00:03:32–00:03:37** probability of understanding something, not an absolute certainty because we're not measuring
**00:03:40–00:03:44** at the tissue level, at the joint level, exactly what's happening. Triangulation is simply the
**00:03:44–00:03:49** process of using multiple points to determine where an object is in space. That concept of
**00:03:49–00:03:55** triangulation, we can use it to evaluate issues from several perspectives, to establish a higher
**00:03:55–00:04:01** probability of what you're saying is real. Let's take a hamstring, for example. We know
**00:04:01–00:04:06** the injury side. We've seen the mechanism, the MRI gives us context, but we're going to use
**00:04:06–00:04:11** multiple tests or perspectives to understand where that's at. Let's go back to
**00:04:13–00:04:18** bicep femteth. We're going to use some eccentric knee flexor strength. We're going to use isometrics
**00:04:18–00:04:24** at our outer range, at inner range. We're going to use those at the hip to understand force
**00:04:24–00:04:28** generating capacity. We're going to jump them on a force plate. We're going to hop them on
**00:04:28–00:04:32** a force plate to try and understand what their stretch shortening cycles like. Have we moved them
**00:04:32–00:04:38** up the chain? We're going to understand what they can do in speed, but we need to understand running
**00:04:38–00:04:43** mechanics profile because we need to understand are they achieving the speeds they're at in a way that
**00:04:43–00:04:51** we would expect. Let's make the point. A single test returning to baseline is not clearance in and
**00:04:51–00:04:57** of itself. It's one data point. That's why we need to get to the skill of understanding
**00:04:57–00:05:02** where we're at. We need to stop speaking in absolutes. In my opinion, it's a bad
**00:05:02–00:05:08** communication pattern. He's high risk. He's ready. This proves neural fatigue. Well, it doesn't.
**00:05:08–00:05:12** We need to talk about what we measured. We measured X, Y, Z. Using these results,

**Source:** Locally transcribed course audio (about 18 minutes). Timestamps are approximate. The transcript is an automated draft and has not been checked against the audio.
The central question is whether the staff have **enough independent, relevant information to act**. The speaker argues that a dramatic single result or initial impression should prompt further investigation, not settle a decision. An evidence stack combines the event or problem history, clinical findings where relevant, an athlete's own prior results, movement and capacity checks, and performance in the conditions the decision concerns.
- **00:00–02:20 — Resist single-signal reactions.** The speaker frames evidence stacking as a way to separate meaningful change from noise and to communicate decisions with appropriate confidence.
- **02:20–10:30 — Soccer injury anecdote.** After an awkward knee injury in an athlete with prior ACL injuries, the speaker describes comparing the initial concern with imaging, clinical examination, movement, a known individual triple-hop baseline, agility, and subsequent training exposure. The point is to update the working assessment as different kinds of evidence arrive. The anecdote does not establish that a hop distance can diagnose an injury or clear an athlete to play.
- **10:30–17:35 — Hamstring return-to-play anecdote.** The speaker describes a second case in which clinical progress and gym measures were supplemented with hopping, running-speed exposure, and a comparison of running mechanics at like-for-like speeds. He emphasizes closing the gap between controlled tests and the demands of the field. The reported return to competition is one case, not a validated return-to-play rule.
- **17:35–18:15 — Leadership application.** Build within-athlete reference points, identify what each new measure adds, and protect the department from changing course on one isolated signal. Ask whether the stack is sufficiently complete for the specific decision.
**Practical takeaway:** Define the decision first, identify the important unanswered questions, then choose measures that add distinct evidence. Medical diagnosis and clearance remain clinical decisions; these stories illustrate the reasoning approach rather than a clinical protocol.

Companion blog post for Podcast 2 
Do We Have SuƯicient Information to Act? 
Building an Evidence Stack to Protect Decision Quality in High-Performance Sport  
One ugly-looking mechanism on video does not automatically equal the worst diagnosis. 
In high-performance environments, the most dangerous decisions are often the fastest ones. A dramatic incident happens, 
emotions spike, and someone calls it early: “He’s out.” “That’s an ACL.” “No chance.” 
This blog supports Podcast 2 in the Decision to Data series and tackles a more useful question than “How much is enough to act?” 
The better question is: 
Do we have suƯicient information to act? 
Because when the pressure is on (from coaches, CEOs, timelines, ﬁnals, contracts), single-signal decisions are where departments 
lose credibility. They are also where athletes lose time, conﬁdence, and sometimes careers. 
What follows is a practical framework for staying clinical when everyone else is reacting. 
The core problem: single-signal decisions under pressure 
In sport, a “signal” can be anything: 
 
a mechanism on video 
 
a player’s reaction 
 
a clinical test 
 
a scan 
 
a hop distance 
 
a single metric from a device 
 
a comment from a coach 
 
your own recent history of injuries in the club 
The mistake is treating one of these as the verdict. 
The better approach is stacking evidence so you can increase the probability that you’re on the right path, and reduce the chance 
that emotion drives the decision. 
This is decision quality. Not as a slogan, but as an operating system. 
Case study 1: the “ACL” that wasn’t an ACL 
Late 2025, just before Christmas, a professional soccer forward (a player I’d previously rehabs through a full ACL reconstruction, 
including a more recent left ACL in 2022) calls after a scary incident. 
What happened (signal #1: mechanism) 
He slid for the ball with the right leg and the left leg got caught underneath and dragged, pulling the knee into valgus. On video, it 
looked ugly. 
But even at this early point, context matters: 
 
the foot was being dragged 
 
he wasn’t clearly weight-bearing 
 
it wasn’t a classic loaded ACL mechanism 
That doesn’t “clear” anything. It simply means you should avoid certainty too early. 
What happened next (signal #2: function in the moment) 
He got up, moved gingerly, then played to half-time. After cooling down and re-warming up, he played the second half. 
That does not equal “no injury.” 
But as a clinical sign, being able to continue playing is meaningful information. 
The immediate bias (what went wrong) 
Post-game, the medical staƯ tested him and went straight to: “You’re out. ACL.” 
Here’s the bias: the team had recently had a couple of ACL injuries. StaƯ were already wound up and paranoid. That emotional state 
makes people jump to the familiar worst-case story. 
Even good clinicians are human. In sport, everyone is under pressure. 
Leadership is staying clinical when others can’t.

Do We Have SuƯicient Information to Act? 
Building an Evidence Stack to Protect Decision Quality in High-Performance Sport  
One ugly-looking mechanism on video does not automatically equal the worst diagnosis. 
In high-performance environments, the most dangerous decisions are often the fastest ones. A dramatic incident happens, 
emotions spike, and someone calls it early: “He’s out.” “That’s an ACL.” “No chance.” 
This blog supports Podcast 2 in the Decision to Data series and tackles a more useful question than “How much is enough to act?” 
The better question is: 
Do we have suƯicient information to act? 
Because when the pressure is on (from coaches, CEOs, timelines, ﬁnals, contracts), single-signal decisions are where departments 
lose credibility. They are also where athletes lose time, conﬁdence, and sometimes careers. 
What follows is a practical framework for staying clinical when everyone else is reacting. 
The core problem: single-signal decisions under pressure 
In sport, a “signal” can be anything: 
 
a mechanism on video 
 
a player’s reaction 
 
a clinical test 
 
a scan 
 
a hop distance 
 
a single metric from a device 
 
a comment from a coach 
 
your own recent history of injuries in the club 
The mistake is treating one of these as the verdict. 
The better approach is stacking evidence so you can increase the probability that you’re on the right path, and reduce the chance 
that emotion drives the decision. 
This is decision quality. Not as a slogan, but as an operating system. 
Case study 1: the “ACL” that wasn’t an ACL 
Late 2025, just before Christmas, a professional soccer forward (a player I’d previously rehabs through a full ACL reconstruction, 
including a more recent left ACL in 2022) calls after a scary incident. 
What happened (signal #1: mechanism) 
He slid for the ball with the right leg and the left leg got caught underneath and dragged, pulling the knee into valgus. On video, it 
looked ugly. 
But even at this early point, context matters: 
 
the foot was being dragged 
 
he wasn’t clearly weight-bearing 
 
it wasn’t a classic loaded ACL mechanism 
That doesn’t “clear” anything. It simply means you should avoid certainty too early. 
What happened next (signal #2: function in the moment) 
He got up, moved gingerly, then played to half-time. After cooling down and re-warming up, he played the second half. 
That does not equal “no injury.” 
But as a clinical sign, being able to continue playing is meaningful information. 
The immediate bias (what went wrong) 
Post-game, the medical staƯ tested him and went straight to: “You’re out. ACL.” 
Here’s the bias: the team had recently had a couple of ACL injuries. StaƯ were already wound up and paranoid. That emotional state 
makes people jump to the familiar worst-case story. 
Even good clinicians are human. In sport, everyone is under pressure. 
Leadership is staying clinical when others can’t.

## Transcript

**00:00–01:24**

G'day, this is Lab 3A in Module 3, writing a Kaigi agenda. So, Kaigi, what's that? Well, Kaigi's a Japanese word for fundamentally a decision meeting. Now, across the course of my career, I had the great experience of working with a particular coach 
who was of Japanese heritage. Now, one of the things that I learned from him was his meeting discipline without question. And it's something I've carried with me throughout my career because as things get more and more complicated, we get more and 
more people, there are different types of meetings. But although he never used the word Kaigi, that's something that I came to study and understand. And it's helped me differentiate what we're doing in meetings and what we need to do to pick up a 
speed. Because again, like we've discussed in other parts of his course, there isn't enough time in our health, in our professional career. We need to move fast and we have to have the information, we have to make good decisions, but we can't sit on 
a fence. And so, within that structure, the Kaigi concept is that we've got a decision-making meeting format. It's built for

**01:24–02:18**

speeds, built for clarity, it's built for accountability, not debate, not ideation or education. So, it allows us to get context. So, let's start with meetings very quickly. There are fundamentally four modalities of meetings. There's a 
decision-making meeting where we need to make a call when options are known. That's principally a Kaigi meeting. There's an info. So, if we're trying to broadcast updates, context, give people information, that's an information meeting. You've got a 
building meeting, which is like creation, whiteboard, iteration, design together, etc. But, if we're looking to make decisions, we've got to go. That's the Kaigi structure. Now, there are two parts to that. There's the fundamental of having that 
structure in the outset, but there's also using it like a samurai sword to cut through where we need to. So, let's have a look at what Kaigi meeting

**02:18–03:16**

fundamentally is. It's really when there's a clear question, very clear to everybody, and it's saving the advance. But, there are two or three realistic options. The information is available, or particularly can be pre-read, and this is something 
we've talked about before and in and out. The notes are associated with these labs. You'll see some of the output, or some of the examples I give from commercial, particularly Amazon, Jeff Bedos, news and formats like this. But, the meeting allows 
alignment, action, but not discussion. There can be some information or argument presented, but it needs to be straightforward. So, the non-negotiables are going to be pre-read. We need to make sure people are coming to the meeting in form. Nothing 
wastes time more in a meeting than, hey, here we go, we can absorb this. Or, the other one, which I believe is a Jeff Bedos one, is when we do PowerPoint presentations, and there's 35,000 slides we need to go through to get. It's got to be cut 
through much, much quicker than that. So, if we're doing

**03:17–03:43**

anything on the board, like, yeah, we can include data analysis, but it has to be explicit about what we know and what we don't know. We can't be giving information, and as we've said in other parts of the course, you're mushing around about what it 
is. We measure this, this is what we've got. That's it. It can't be inferring anything that we don't really know. Timeboxing is another important part of the KG meeting. Keep contributions short. Now, different people,

**03:43–04:48**

different literature references different things. 120 seconds, I'll show you a 30 second version later on, but you've got a timeframe. I was in a meeting recently with a colleague of mine I've known for a long time. He doesn't specifically know any 
of this stuff, but he came to your meeting and he said, Rob, we're going to do this task, and you've got 60 seconds. Initially, I was like, whoa, I got into the hang of it very, very quickly, and I thought it was an economic meeting. I thought it 
was extraordinarily good, and it was like cut to the chase, like really get down the points that matter and don't buck around. It was awesome. It was really awesome, and he continued to work through that process at the moment. I thought at that 
meeting, it reflected back on meetings I've used for trying to explain the moment. I think that timeboxing is super important. It puts pressure on people to convey the information that we need, the critical information, and that's it. No more. If 
there's more detail in pre-reading, make sure people got it in advance.

**04:48–05:56**

The next part of the KG meetings, there's the strict outputs, so decision logs. Every meeting's got to have a decision log. This is something I think I didn't do well early in my career, and I'm trying to do far better now, is go through and like, 
what was the outcome of the meeting? Not guessing it, action, due date, owner, whose is it? Review method, review date, and that's logged in an audit trail. We know at the end of it, it's not like, hey, you know when everything hits the fan, you 
know you guys with that meeting, and we said we'd do this, and we go, I don't remember that. We log it down, and we log it in a circular. A little bit of admin. It is a little bit of admin, but I will say it's worth the cost. I say this with a lot 
of things in this area. If you don't get anything for free, nothing comes for free. If you want a better audit trail, and you want to keep things accountable, and maybe for leaders, it becomes challenging, because you're in so many meetings that 
hold so many things, is get it written down. Maybe there's an opportunity in that to have part of your staff say, you're on audits today, bang, fill it out, get it done, get it to me. That's a part of it, because then that person is learning those 
components that they would use later on.

**05:56–07:27**

Let's be clear, though. Let's be real clear. Kage format is not for everything, but there are times when we need to go slower, when we need to ideate on a problem, when we need to brainstorm, where we need to get the butchers paper out in the wall 
or the white board. That's when we need to take a time. Different format. Same thing with education components or training discussions. I wouldn't use this format. I don't use this format in staff meetings. I tend to find them demo my informing 
meetings, but also I use them heavily as staff education, so they're not at that tempo. However, I will ensure that on certain things, there are reading that's required before we come in the meeting. Don't come in the meeting ill prepared, because 
as the person running the meeting, I have to do work to get ready. If you want a good staff meeting, and you want good engagement, like as a staff member, and you get that in feedback periodically, could we have more information yet? I'm going to 
give you more, but I want more. Again, nothing comes for free. You need to put in work to get quality back, that type of thing. When we're looking again, things you're not great at, complex technical design or complex technical discussions, that's 
not that space. Again, I'd always specify that if we're in those types of meetings, that people get in front of what we're doing. You think when you've got vague problems, I would be pushing them out, particularly when there's questions that aren't 
hard. I don't push them to another format. Let's have a look at two

**07:28–08:36**

examples where I've used other KV format. The first one, and I think this one is critically important, this is what I call a go no-go meeting. For many years in the AFL, we would have the athletes come in the morning, prep, and we would be looking 
for a start, whatever it was. Go on the field by 9, 9.30, warm up, everything's done, and we're into the body of the session. As most teams would do, players come in in the morning, there would be straining components and monitoring bits and pieces 
and whatever. Now, I have another whole section on the philosophy of how I organized all of that, which is quite different. We're not cutting all that off, but if you can imagine, we've got this body of information that has to be sorted in a certain 
way. Within that structure, the way I set up my teams was, again, subject for another time, but every group, everyone was in pairs at SDC and Ephesia, so to speak, and everybody has a responsibility to answer information, have difficult information 
for that player.

**08:36–09:12**

As the management, as the HPM, I would oversee a lot of the data coming through, so I would also have an opinion on the data coming through now. I've seen the data, the coach and Ephesia may have seen the player, may have spoken to them, so that's 
the immediate responsibility. Then the broad responsibilities, everybody on staff, as the responsibility, that if they've seen something in the morning, in that process, they've seen somebody warming up reading, they've seen somebody stretching, not 
the way they would normally do it, or a little bit more, or behaving a little bit differently, speaking a bit differently. In some cases, they're stressing differently, and we'll come to that in another episode.

**09:13–10:19**

However, the point of this for us, that we go to a no-go, no-go meeting, it would be right, we're on, go. I would read the top name, Joe Abrams, number one. I'm asking a question. When I put that name up, I'm asking a question. If there's any data 
associated with it, I would be saying, hey, that guy's ground score is down a long way. Issues, what do we got? What we do is we stack information. Now, we talk about this in, I think we did in module two, about stacking evidence. That's what we're 
trying to do. I'm not going to pull in and out of training based on one thing, but here's where the speed in the caving comes in, is everybody's responsibility is to respond quickly. In order, go, no-go, name. If I don't say something within two 
seconds, next one is to the physio, the responsible physio and strength condition. Got to come straight for the party. I've seen this, this, and this. Right, anybody else? I don't want to be saying, hey, anybody else. Then everybody else's 
responsibility is if I've seen something to drag in, so then my job at the top of the tree is to go, we have all bits of evidence there. I might mark that for follow-up meeting, us at the meeting, down the seas, fast.

**10:19–11:21**

We want to be, we got 50 players, we want to be tracking through, we're going to get this down to kind of like less than 30 seconds per player. Because if there's no, if a player is clear on everything and their behavior, there's nothing untoward. 
Don't say anything. Good, negative space. We move on to the next thing. We move quickly. That was our go, no-go meeting. But at the end of it, it was very clear. This player, they might be, let's say we had four players you wanted to review. Let's 
say two of them were medically orientated, and one might have been psychologically orientated because they were, there was a mental health issue. They were often maybe worried about something, whatever. So I might go, one, two, three, head physio, 
go. He walks straight out the door and he's on to those three. The mental health issue, psych, bang, go. Report back to me. They all knew they got to be back to me within 20 minutes because then I could report through the coach. So I would then go 
to the coach, give him a preliminary clearance meeting to say, hey, we're good. We've got four guys, we're checking on, 20 minutes, we'll get there. So everybody knows what's going on.

**11:21–12:13**

We've got everybody involved and it's fast. That's one of my most effective, and I used that for quite a number of years. And I could put, I think we ended up having, we had like 15, 17 people in that meeting, but everyone stood and it was fast. And 
you didn't say boo, unless you had something. But everybody was encouraged to bring something. If there was something there, because there are nuances. And what you do again in my monitoring structure is we're looking for a web. If you imagine 
layers of information, we're going to catch them at different layers. Now, if you only have one layer, like a sieve or something like that, certain information might pass through. We want to have multiple layers. So we're going to catch all the 
pertinent information and put it together and see what it means. Anyway, so that's that KD format that I use there. The other way I use it more recently is as a

**12:14–13:23**

30 second move. So you're in a meeting where you're doing some problem solving, it's bigger, but it's getting stuck. We go, right, we're going KD, 10 minutes, right, decision, ownership, decide, move on. And that's, in a way, getting people to 
change gears. Because they know what I'm talking about is, right, we need something here. This isn't going to go on forever. We can't be here all day. Make a call. Let's get on with it. And that then comes back to your leadership pattern and style a 
little bit too, which again, is subject for another component. But you get the idea, hopefully, you get it, that this KD structure allows people to know, that's it. We're not mucking around anymore. What's your point? Bang, bang, bang, bang, let's 
bring together a decision, go on it, move on. Let's get through it. So this is how we start to understand efficiency and getting things to move because we've got ourselves and our staff that all know what's going on. So from a leadership 
perspective, we can later on develop their perspectives to a point, but then we force consensus at that point of impasse. We get a clean mechanism, we decide, document, move on. All right, good luck.

######## Lab_3a_Blog_Kaigi_agendas
=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Lab 3A Blog  
Kaigi agendas: how to make decisions fast without 
creating chaos 
Most performance departments don’t have a “meeting problem”. 
They have a meeting-type problem. 
People turn up to the wrong kind of meeting, with the wrong expectation, and then wonder why nothing 
gets done. 
So, here’s a simple framework that keeps teams moving. 
The four modalities of meetings 
Every meeting you run should have one primary job: 
 
Decide — make a call and align everyone 
 
Diagnose — understand the problem and its drivers 
 
Inform — distribute updates and context 
 
Build — create, design, iterate, develop 
If you don’t name the modality, you’ll drift. And drift is where time disappears. 
Where Kaigi ﬁts 
Kaigi is the tool for Decide. 
It’s designed for moments where: 
 
the question is clear, 
 
the options are limited (usually 2–3), 
 
and the team needs alignment quickly. 
Kaigi isn’t about “more discussion”. 
It’s about less ambiguity. 
The Kaigi prerequisites (non-negotiables) 
A Kaigi meeting only works if you respect the rules. 
1) A clear question 
If the question is vague, Kaigi fails. Vague belongs in Diagnose or Build. 
2) Limited options 
If you’ve got six options, you don’t have options — you have uncertainty. That’s Diagnose. 
3) Pre-read (when possible) 
The best Kaigi meetings happen before the meeting: 
 
send the information, 
 
include the analysis, 
 
and be explicit about what you know and what you don’t. 
If people arrive cold, you’re not deciding — you’re catching up. 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
4) Time-boxing 
Kaigi runs on tempo. You referenced 120 seconds as a typical limit. 
In pre-training environments, it can be even tighter: 30 seconds per point. 
If someone can’t land the point quickly, it’s probably not ready. Take it oƯline. 
5) Strict outputs: the decision log 
Kaigi without a decision log is just a fast meeting that creates slow confusion later. 
Every Kaigi output needs: 
 
Owner (who owns it) 
 
Action (what happens) 
 
Due date (by when) 
 
Review process (how we’ll check it) 
 
Recorded in a decision log (audit trail) 
That audit trail matters. It protects staƯ, improves clarity, and stops decisions being re-litigated 
every week. 
Two high-performance use cases 
1) Pre-training go / no-go 
This is where Kaigi shines. 
You’ve got multiple feeds coming in quickly: 
 
sports science data, 
 
testing information, 
 
physio input and manual assessment, 
 
sometimes coaching constraints. 
A compressed Kaigi structure keeps it clean: 
 
bring the information, 
 
make the point, 
 
decide, 
 
log it, 
 
move. 
Anything incomplete or speculative goes oƯline. 
2) Switching modes when a meeting hits an impasse 
Problem-solving meetings (Diagnose) are valuable — but they can stall when perspectives collide. 
A practical move is to declare a mode change late in the meeting: 
“We’re moving from Diagnose to Kaigi for the last 10–15 minutes.” 
Now the job is not to explore. The job is to decide: 
 
assign responsibility (often discipline lead), 
 
select the option, 
 
record it, 
 
move forward. 
What Kaigi is not for 
Kaigi is not an education session. 
It’s not an ideation workshop. 
It’s not a design studio. 
And it’s not the right place for complex work when the information isn’t ready. 
=== PAGE 3 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Kaigi is a decision engine — and decision engines only run cleanly on prepared fuel. 
The punchline 
If you want speed, you need structure. 
If you want accountability, you need a log. 
If you want fewer meetings, you need the right meeting type. 
Kaigi isn’t magic. 
It’s just discipline — written down. 
######## Lab_3b_Blog_Meeting_typology
=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Lab 3b Blog  
Meeting typology: the right room for the right job 
A lot of “meeting problems” in high performance aren’t really meeting problems. 
They’re meeting-type problems. 
People walk into a room expecting diƯerent outcomes: 
 
one person thinks it’s a decision meeting, 
 
another thinks it’s brainstorming, 
 
someone else thinks it’s an update, 
 
and a few people assume it’s an injury review. 
The result is predictable: drift, frustration, and slow execution. 
Meeting typology ﬁxes this. It’s simply the discipline of choosing the right meeting for the job. 
And as strange as it sounds: discipline breeds freedom. 
When the meeting type is clear, people prepare properly, creativity has a place, and decisions 
don’t take three weeks. 
Start with four modes 
Most meetings ﬁt into one of four modalities: 
 
Decide — commit to action 
 
Diagnose — understand a known problem and test hypotheses 
 
Inform — broadcast updates and context 
 
Build — co-create and design solutions 
If you name the modality up front, the meeting immediately becomes easier to run. 
Decide: Kaigi 
Kaigi is your “Decide” format. 
It works when: 
 
the question is clear, 
 
the options are limited, 
 
and you need alignment quickly. 
It only stays clean if you respect the basics: 
 
pre-read where possible, 
 
strict time-boxing, 
 
and strict outputs captured in a decision log (owner, action, due date, review). 
Diagnose: the problem-solving meeting 
This is the classic 30-minute multidisciplinary meeting: 
performance, medical, sometimes coaching. 
The problem is known, but the solution isn’t. 
These meetings can be high value — and they can also become a time sink if you let them 
wander. The controls are simple: 
 
agree in advance what problems you’re discussing, 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
 
allocate time per item, 
 
and if you don’t have enough information, don’t pretend you do. 
A practical pattern is: 
Diagnose → assign a small group to gather missing information → return inside a deﬁned window 
→ then use Kaigi to decide. 
Inform: broadcast meetings (and the trap) 
Inform meetings are not bad. They’re necessary. 
The trap is when information meetings become accidental problem-solving sessions. 
That usually happens when a key stakeholder isn’t across the detail and the group starts re-
explaining everything in real time. 
If someone needs a catch-up, keep it targeted: one meeting, one stakeholder, one or two core 
staƯ. Don’t make it a department-wide drag on momentum. 
Ops: inform and unblock (with Kaigi tempo) 
Ops or stand-ups are about speed: 
 
what’s happening, 
 
what’s blocked, 
 
who owns it, 
 
what’s next. 
They should feel Kaigi-like: short, clear, action-oriented. 
If ops meetings expand into problem solving, you’ve lost the point. 
Build: design and co-creation 
Build meetings are where you change systems: 
training structure, workﬂow, rehab process, communication ﬂow. 
They need more space — less pressure — because you’re creating, not committing. 
But there’s a key move here: build meetings often need to ﬁnish with a Decide step. Otherwise 
you’ve created ideas, not outcomes. 
Learn: After Action and Postmortem 
After Action and Postmortem meetings are learning engines — if they remain blameless. 
The rules are: 
 
stick to timelines, facts, and metrics, 
 
be honest about what you can measure and what you can’t, 
 
and treat learning as the goal, not accountability theatre. 
If you want a performance department that improves over time, these meetings aren’t optional. 
=== PAGE 3 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
The punchline 
Before you write the agenda, choose the room. 
Name the modality. 
Deﬁne the output. 
Time-box it. 
Capture the decision or the learning. 
That’s how you move fast — and keep everyone conﬁdent in what’s happening.

explaining everything in real time. 
If someone needs a catch-up, keep it targeted: one meeting, one stakeholder, one or two core 
staƯ. Don’t make it a department-wide drag on momentum. 
Ops: inform and unblock (with Kaigi tempo) 
Ops or stand-ups are about speed: 
 
what’s happening, 
 
what’s blocked, 
 
who owns it, 
 
what’s next. 
They should feel Kaigi-like: short, clear, action-oriented. 
If ops meetings expand into problem solving, you’ve lost the point. 
Build: design and co-creation 
Build meetings are where you change systems: 
training structure, workﬂow, rehab process, communication ﬂow. 
They need more space — less pressure — because you’re creating, not committing.

After Action and Postmortem meetings are learning engines — if they remain blameless. 
The rules are: 
 
stick to timelines, facts, and metrics, 
 
be honest about what you can measure and what you can’t, 
 
and treat learning as the goal, not accountability theatre. 
If you want a performance department that improves over time, these meetings aren’t optional.

## Main point
Select and announce a meeting's purpose before setting its agenda. The speaker argues that clearly named meeting modes improve preparation, protect creative work from premature decisions, and make decisions faster when the options are known. A staff meeting may include several modes, provided each segment has a stated purpose and expected output.
## Meeting modes
| Mode | Use it for | Structure and expected result |
| --- | --- | --- |

| **Inform** | Sharing updates and context | Keep the goal to information sharing. The speaker warns that such meetings can drift into unplanned problem-solving. (04:37–05:02) |
| **Build** | Co-creating or redesigning a system, structure, or training week | Give people room to contribute, consider psychological safety, and allow time to digest ideas. Some projects may need several meetings rather than one immediate decision. (05:34–06:18) |

- **Mixed staff meetings (04:03–04:37):** One agenda can move through inform, diagnose, and decide segments. Define the segment boundaries so participants know which kind of contribution is needed.

## Main idea
Stoplight Storytelling is a short, repeatable presentation format for decisions. The speaker wants staff to state the question, show the relevant signal clearly, recommend a direction, and record the resulting action. The format is meant to keep a sequence of presentations from expanding into long, unfocused discussions. (00:00–01:15)
## Suggested slide structure
1. **Question or headline.** State the issue the group must address, rather than opening with data without a purpose. (01:41–02:17)
2. **Status.** Use green for go, amber for hold or monitor, and red for stop or change. (02:17–02:27)
3. **Evidence.** Use at most one chart, readable immediately by everyone in the room. Explain whether an observed difference is meaningful relative to measurement error, normal variation, and other convergent evidence. (02:27–03:02; 03:45–04:25)
4. **Request and accountability.** Ask for a start, stop, or change decision. End with one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point, recorded in the decision log. (03:02–03:45)
## Presentation rules
- Keep the message short, label axes and differences clearly, and choose visual encodings that are unambiguous. The speaker cautions against dual axes and complex charts that need extended explanation. (04:25–05:51)
- Avoid multiple charts, multiple requests, and brand-new information during the presentation. Every status, including amber, needs a next action or review date. (05:51–06:23)
- A roughly two-minute presentation can be a benchmark, but novel or complex issues may require pre-reading or a separate meeting for collaborative work. (06:23–06:43)
- The required close is a direction—go, hold, or stop—plus a documented action and review checkpoint. (06:43–06:56)
## Operational use
The speaker argues that a shared format lets staff present more autonomously and makes a series of short presentations manageable in one meeting. The timing and efficiency claims are examples from his practice, not validated thresholds. (06:56–07:54)
**Practical template:** Question → green/amber/red status → one clear chart with uncertainty and supporting context → requested direction → owner, due date, and review.

=== PAGE 1 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Lab 3C Blog  
Stoplight storytelling: faster calls, fewer debates, clean 
audit trails 
If you want meetings to move faster, you don’t start by demanding speed. 
You start by improving how people present information. 
Because most debate in performance environments isn’t caused by disagreement. 
It’s caused by unclear briefs. 
Stoplight storytelling is a simple method that ﬁxes that. 
What stoplight storytelling is 
Stoplight storytelling is a one-slide decision brief that uses a Green / Amber / Red status to 
force clarity: 
 
Green: we’re good — continue 
 
Amber: hold — monitor — review soon 
 
Red: stop or change — act now 
It’s designed to sit inside Kaigi-style decision meetings, where tempo matters and outcomes 
must be logged. 
When to use it 
Stoplight storytelling works best at decision gates — especially operational ones. 
Examples: 
 
“Do we change this drill?” 
 
“Are we adjusting speed exposure this week?” 
 
“Do we keep this procedure or stop it?” 
The key is that the question is clear, and you’re asking for a decision, not a discussion. 
The one-slide anatomy 
A stoplight slide has six parts: 
1. Headline — what are we deciding? 
2. Stoplight status — Green/Amber/Red 
3. One chart — maximum 
4. Signal vs noise — shown against SEM and MDC so we’re not reacting to ﬂuctuations 
5. One ask — written as a verb: Start / Stop / Change / Limit 
6. Accountability — owner, action, due date, review date — and logged. 
That’s it. 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
If you need more than one chart, more than one ask, or more than two minutes to explain it, 
you’re not in stoplight territory anymore. You’re in a Diagnose or Build meeting. 
Signal, noise, and conﬁdence 
The discipline here is non-negotiable: 
If the change doesn’t exceed system noise, don’t dress it up as insight. 
Tie conﬁdence to the statistics you have: 
 
standard error (SEM), 
 
minimal detectable change (MDC). 
And if you have convergent evidence — two small pieces that point the same way — use it. But 
keep it tight. This format is not built for data dumps. 
The common failure: pretty but not useful 
Stoplight slides fail when the chart looks good but can’t be read quickly. 
The rules are simple: 
 
axes labelled, 
 
diƯerences labelled, 
 
visually clear at a glance, 
 
no distracting visuals. 
Clarity beats sophistication in decision meetings. 
The most important rule: nothing hangs 
Even Amber must have a plan. 
“Hold” is not an outcome unless you attach: 
 
what you’re monitoring, 
 
who owns it, 
 
and when it will be reviewed (e.g., 48 hours). 
If actions hang, decisions drag. And when decisions drag, you lose tempo — and you lose 
control of the system. 
The punchline 
Stoplight storytelling is how you build a culture of: 
 
faster calls, 
 
fewer debates, 
 
and a clean audit trail. 
It’s not about being aggressive. 
It’s about being clear. 
And in high performance, clarity is a competitive advantage.
