Lab 3D Blog  
Meetings as an education tool: the easiest way to develop leadership 
Most performance departments treat meetings as a necessary evil. 
That’s a mistake. 
Meetings are one of the best leadership development tools you’ve got — because they create a 
repeatable, observable opportunity for staƯ to practise the behaviours you actually need in high 
performance: 
 
preparation 
 
clarity 
 
decision discipline 
 
follow-up 
Give staƯ meetings to run 
If you’re senior staƯ and you want your team to grow, don’t just “mentor” them. Give them 
ownership. 
Let them run meetings. 
Done well, it’s empowering. StaƯ feel trusted, and they learn what it means to lead a process — 
not just contribute an opinion. 
Guardrails create freedom 
This only works if the meeting has structure. 
Use clear meeting deﬁnitions and templates (Kaigi principles are a good example): 
 
what the meeting is for 
 
what the agenda is 
 
how long it runs 
 
what the outputs must be 
 
how actions are tracked 
That’s the key: discipline breeds freedom. 
When people know the rules, they can move quickly and still create solutions inside the bounds 
of the system. 
Think of it as: 
 
leadership sets the six-lane highway (strategy) 
 
staƯ choose when to change lanes (tactics) 
…but nobody drives oƯ-road. 
Don’t avoid the quiet staƯ — develop them 
Some staƯ don’t like public speaking. That’s normal. 
The answer isn’t to protect them from meetings. The answer is to scaƯold practice: 
 
start with a simple meeting 
 
give them one topic, one slide, one clear time box 
 
debrief afterwards 
 
repeat 
=== PAGE 2 ===
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE 2026 
Conﬁdence doesn’t arrive ﬁrst. Repetition arrives ﬁrst. 
A message to young practitioners 
If you want to move forward, look for reps. 
Ask your boss for the chance to run a meeting. 
It forces you to learn: 
 
how to structure time 
 
how to clarify the objective 
 
how to land an outcome 
 
how to follow up 
Those are leadership skills. And leadership skills are rarely taught — they’re practised. 
The punchline 
The biggest challenge in developing leaders is opportunity. 
Meetings create opportunity. 
They create reps. 
And reps create leadership. 
And one more thing that CEO’s do… 
Meetings are an opportunity to test your thinking. 
Avoid excessive bias by having your staƯ argue speciﬁc aspects of an issue. 
Even ones that may not speciﬁcally side with. 
Carefully consider each perspective and evaluate it against your own. 
A simple method is to pose the problem…then sit quietly under someone starts. 
Be careful this method may make some uncomfortable.

Source: downloaded Lab 3D video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft; this summary reports the speaker's approach rather than independently validating its effects.
## Main idea
The speaker treats running a meeting as a practical leadership exercise. Giving staff ownership of a meeting lets them practice structure, concise communication, follow-up, and accountability while building confidence. He describes assigning a medical review meeting to his head physiotherapist as one example. (00:46–02:25)
## How to use it
- Define the meeting's purpose and keep an agenda, time limits, and agreed decision boundaries. Record an owner, action, due date, and review point for each output. Give staff room to make tactical choices within the larger strategy. (02:25–03:11)
- Make participation deliberate. Track who contributes, invite quieter staff in, and give them notice when they will be asked to present. For less confident speakers, start with a small meeting, one slide, one topic, and a short time slot, then increase responsibility. (03:11–05:09)
- Staff seeking leadership experience can offer to run a small meeting, using it to practice directing information and keeping the group focused. (05:09–06:14)
## A use for senior leaders
The speaker describes leaders stating a problem and then pausing to hear staff views before offering their own, so their opinion does not dominate the discussion. He sometimes asks someone to prepare an opposing case with evidence. The resulting debate helps him test his assumptions before a decision. (06:14–08:49)
**Practical takeaway:** Assign clear meeting ownership, support the facilitator with structure, and use discussion to develop staff judgment and challenge the leader's own view.

**00:01:17–00:01:22** part of that process and you get them. Particularly on the follow up sort of habits. You know,

**00:01:27–00:01:32** a bit of work. That's not a bad one. You know, getting a direct assistant, getting someone
**00:01:32–00:01:36** who's going to sit in your pocket to do some of that stuff. The trade off is their

**00:01:40–00:01:46** one, and this is probably a no brainer for everybody, is build confidence and staff feel
**00:01:46–00:01:52** trusted and empowered. I made a habit in my 12 years I was in the AFL where I had a big

**00:02:20–00:02:25** staff are on that same wavelength with you. So the guardrails, like keep it efficient,
**00:02:25–00:02:30** keep the structured principles, define the meeting types and purposes we've done, clear
**00:02:30–00:02:34** agendas, time boxes, we've talked about, capture your outputs due to the owner action, due
**00:02:34–00:02:40** date, review, how does that operate? Make sure we stick within agreed guidelines. When
**00:02:40–00:02:44** we talk about that, we've got to make sure that strategically our staff are on board
**00:02:44–00:02:50** with us. So this is that idea again of strategy versus tactics, that we're going to give them
**00:02:50–00:02:55** the opportunity like a guardra, we've used that terminology to operate in that space and
**00:02:55–00:03:00** within that, they're going to make their tactical changes. So as a staff member gets
**00:03:00–00:03:06** made more experienced, stronger, they can certainly utilize meetings to expand and practice
**00:03:06–00:03:11** and develop some ideas. One of the things you will come across is staff who don't like

**00:04:14–00:04:18** coach, someone's doing a track cycling, something like that, they might do some

**00:04:23–00:04:28** Great. But you're going to present it. You've got to come in, present again, we give strict
**00:04:28–00:04:33** guidelines and we run through it. So I think the idea there is don't avoid those who can't

**00:04:37–00:04:42** slide, one topic, all that, just progress it through a limited time. But I really
**00:04:42–00:04:48** think that needs to be done. And I think if we're in that position where young
**00:04:48–00:04:51** practitioners are saying, particularly in a job review and review, say the end of the
**00:04:51–00:04:55** year, their position review, hey, you know, I really want to become a leader. Well,

**00:05:13–00:05:17** career practitioners listening to this. I think this is an opportunity. So if you're
**00:05:17–00:05:22** trying to push up the next tier, one of the key things is to go to your boss and say,
**00:05:22–00:05:26** opportunity is I can lead a meeting for you. Let me like, give me the smallest thing,
**00:05:26–00:05:31** but get the hang of it. I get the hang of starting to direct information, be clear,
**00:05:31–00:05:37** concise, stick to the project, etc, and get it done. You know, so it's really practice reps for
**00:05:37–00:05:41** leadership preparation, they get through, make sure they're following structure,
**00:05:41–00:05:48** all the things we've talked about. So to wrap this, this lab up, I think from that
**00:05:49–00:05:54** opportunity perspective, leadership is really about lack of practice of opportunities. It's
**00:05:54–00:05:58** very hard when you're in a, you're a high performance manager, leading department to
**00:05:58–00:06:03** get someone in to experience the things that you experience all the time, because there's
**00:06:03–00:06:09** conversations you can't bring anyone into, but it means a great opportunity to let staff practice
**00:06:09–00:06:14** and get around there. From that perspective, I'm going to twist the wheel now just to give
**00:06:14–00:06:18** you a little bit of a wrap up on something a little bit different. One of the things I've
**00:06:18–00:06:25** seen over time is how really experienced operators, CEOs, and particularly some of the really
**00:06:25–00:06:31** effective senior coaches I've worked with over time, how they run meetings. One in particular
**00:06:31–00:06:37** was very good at coming in, we'd have an agenda, we'd have all that, and he would talk through
**00:06:37–00:06:43** and he'd go, here's the problem, and he would stop, he would stop call, and he would literally sit
**00:06:43–00:06:50** there and wait, because what he's trying to do was generate conversations and generate input from
**00:06:50–00:06:57** people. Everybody on a given problem, particularly a leader, is going to have a view. Now what you
**00:06:57–00:07:04** want to test as a leader, you want to make sure that you're not biasing a decision with your
**00:07:04–00:07:08** opinion. You want to make sure that you've got a balanced perspective, and one of the easiest ways
**00:07:08–00:07:14** to do that is to get your staff to argue out, to discuss, bring a point. Interestingly, one of
**00:07:14–00:07:21** the things that I certainly do now with my staff is I might bring up a point, and we might have
**00:07:21–00:07:24** something we're going to a meeting, and we have a subject that we're on, so everyone's coming in a
**00:07:24–00:07:30** little bit prepared, but I will speak to one of them, and I'll say your job is to come in and
**00:07:30–00:07:37** argue the opposite. Find data, find anything to argue the opposite if you can. Argue a particular
**00:07:37–00:07:43** aspect, which might be a lesser focus point, but you're getting someone to create an argument,
**00:07:43–00:07:48** because when we can work through an argument, and we can logically debate it, and we can bring
**00:07:48–00:07:53** a good argument forward and come to a great perspective, we have real resolve and real
**00:07:53–00:07:59** strength around that decision. Now, as a leader, what you want to do is get your people who are
**00:07:59–00:08:05** good practitioners and operators to bring those points, and internally, while I'm sitting here
**00:08:05–00:08:11** listening, I'm testing my own thoughts on this. So evaluating, have I considered that? Have I
**00:08:11–00:08:18** considered A, B, C, D? So a meeting is an exceptional place, exceptional place for you to
**00:08:18–00:08:23** challenge your own ideas, and to make sure that you're evaluating things effectively, because
**00:08:23–00:08:29** as I said, we all become biased, and we want to try and beat that. So wrap that up. Meeting's a
**00:08:29–00:08:35** great learning opportunity for your staff, so for you, for leadership to push down and pull the
**00:08:36–00:08:40** younger ones up, but equally for the younger ones to make sure you're aware that it's
**00:08:40–00:08:44** an opportunity to go up, to go looking for that opportunity. And the last one is for everybody
**00:08:44–00:08:49** running a meeting, to use it to get the ideas out of other people as you're moving towards
**00:08:49–00:08:51** a decision. Anyway, I hope you got something out of that. Good luck.

**00:05:41–00:05:48** all the things we've talked about. So to wrap this, this lab up, I think from that
**00:05:49–00:05:54** opportunity perspective, leadership is really about lack of practice of opportunities. It's
**00:05:54–00:05:58** very hard when you're in a, you're a high performance manager, leading department to
**00:05:58–00:06:03** get someone in to experience the things that you experience all the time, because there's
**00:06:03–00:06:09** conversations you can't bring anyone into, but it means a great opportunity to let staff practice
**00:06:09–00:06:14** and get around there. From that perspective, I'm going to twist the wheel now just to give
**00:06:14–00:06:18** you a little bit of a wrap up on something a little bit different. One of the things I've
**00:06:18–00:06:25** seen over time is how really experienced operators, CEOs, and particularly some of the really
**00:06:25–00:06:31** effective senior coaches I've worked with over time, how they run meetings. One in particular
**00:06:31–00:06:37** was very good at coming in, we'd have an agenda, we'd have all that, and he would talk through
**00:06:37–00:06:43** and he'd go, here's the problem, and he would stop, he would stop call, and he would literally sit
**00:06:43–00:06:50** there and wait, because what he's trying to do was generate conversations and generate input from
**00:06:50–00:06:57** people. Everybody on a given problem, particularly a leader, is going to have a view. Now what you

**00:07:08–00:07:14** to do that is to get your staff to argue out, to discuss, bring a point. Interestingly, one of
**00:07:14–00:07:21** the things that I certainly do now with my staff is I might bring up a point, and we might have
**00:07:21–00:07:24** something we're going to a meeting, and we have a subject that we're on, so everyone's coming in a

**00:07:30–00:07:37** argue the opposite. Find data, find anything to argue the opposite if you can. Argue a particular
**00:07:37–00:07:43** aspect, which might be a lesser focus point, but you're getting someone to create an argument,
**00:07:43–00:07:48** because when we can work through an argument, and we can logically debate it, and we can bring
**00:07:48–00:07:53** a good argument forward and come to a great perspective, we have real resolve and real
**00:07:53–00:07:59** strength around that decision. Now, as a leader, what you want to do is get your people who are

**00:08:05–00:08:11** listening, I'm testing my own thoughts on this. So evaluating, have I considered that? Have I

The speaker urges leaders to make time outside daily operations to ask what could derail a plan or expose a weakness in the department's system. A team can share a common process and still overlook an important alternative, especially under time pressure. (00:00–01:41; 03:22–04:06)
## Ways to challenge a plan
- Assign someone to argue against the group's favored explanation or proposal. The speaker uses the “tenth man” idea from *World War Z* as a memorable example of deliberate dissent. The film and historical references are illustrations here, not evidence for a particular decision method. (01:42–04:00)
- Let team members offer their perspectives before the leader speaks, then test the proposed approach with specific questions. The speaker describes a coach who listened quietly before asking where a plan might fail. (04:59–06:34)
- Deliberately switch viewpoints: examine the facts apart from the pressure surrounding a decision, then consider how it looks to the athlete and other stakeholders. The speaker connects this to Edward de Bono's “six hats” idea. (06:34–08:04)
He recounts a period of repeated calf problems in an AFL team and says the group changed course only after a doctor delivered a message the coach could accept. This is a personal account of decision dynamics; the transcript does not establish the injuries' cause or the effect of the training change. (08:04–10:00)
**Practical takeaway:** Set aside regular time to review an apparently stable system, identify what could go wrong, and revise it as staff, technology, and knowledge change. (11:13–13:58)

**00:00:21–00:00:30** end of the Data to Decisions project. Now, what I want to finish off with is an absolutely critical
**00:00:30–00:00:35** piece of thinking. This is called structured thinking under pressure. But what are we doing
**00:00:35–00:00:41** it for? We're trying to figure out and understand, see in advance, if you like, things we've missed.
**00:00:41–00:00:46** Something I've talked about over time with different people is the ability to see around
**00:00:46–00:00:52** corners is the thing that makes a difference in leadership. The ability to understand maybe what's
**00:00:52–00:00:57** coming next to identify things that others didn't see. To do something that's different to run of
**00:00:57–00:01:04** the mill because you've identified an opportunity. Now, the question is, how do we do that? In the
**00:01:04–00:01:10** busy world, particularly of sport, where you're often on the treadmill, and this is when this
**00:01:10–00:01:16** treadmill situation occurs, one thing to think about is what we call an entrepreneurism working on
**00:01:16–00:01:20** the business or in the business. Now, quite often we get caught in a lot of the stuff we've been
**00:01:20–00:01:25** talked about throughout the course of Data to Decisions has been about getting processes
**00:01:25–00:01:30** in place. We're going to work in the business. But working on the business is going to maybe
**00:01:30–00:01:36** be about you thinking. Maybe it's going to be you taking a step outside of the processes
**00:01:36–00:01:41** you build to try and understand where the gaps are, where's the weak point. As I mentioned in
**00:01:42–00:01:49** a section quite some time back, I was asked in a meeting by a very solid associate of mine,
**00:01:49–00:01:55** said literally, what can fuck this up? Tell me now, let's go really short and fast. What
**00:01:55–00:02:02** could derail the situation? What we're going to talk about is World War Z. The 2013 movie called
**00:02:02–00:02:09** World War Z starred Brad Pitt, a fundamentally zombie movie, great movie. However, in that
**00:02:09–00:02:15** movie, they talked about what they call the 10th man rule. The 10th man rule, Brad Pitt's
**00:02:15–00:02:21** character gets to Israel and Israel then be besieged by the last holdouts of the against
**00:02:21–00:02:25** the zombies because of the wall city. Anyway, the long story short is they kind of knew it
**00:02:25–00:02:29** was coming in and taken some steps and Brad Pitt's character says like, how did you know?
**00:02:29–00:02:38** And this guy says, well, this Mossad officer says, well, we looked at what could challenge us
**00:02:38–00:02:43** in the future as a country. And this was one of the things we came up with. And fundamentally,
**00:02:43–00:02:49** they'd said that this Mossad agent had been designated the 10th man. So the 10th man rule
**00:02:49–00:02:55** was that he had to argue against everything that the group had come up with. So the group
**00:02:55–00:03:00** thing. Now, as much as this was dramatized in the movie, it is actually a real thing.
**00:03:00–00:03:06** After 1973, Yom Kippur walled, the Israelis came up with the devil's advocate unit. And the
**00:03:06–00:03:10** devil's advocate unit is designed for that to look at things that are outside the box
**00:03:10–00:03:16** to the unlikely scenarios, the low probability things, what could happen? Essentially, answer
**00:03:16–00:03:22** the question, what could fuck this up? Now, I think that is such a simple approach. But
**00:03:22–00:03:26** it's a hard one. It's a really hard one. Brute think when everyone's kind of agreeing
**00:03:26–00:03:31** and getting along is kind of what some ways have been advocating for in other parts
**00:03:31–00:03:35** of this course, trying to think about how do we get people on the same page? How do
**00:03:35–00:03:40** we get people living on the same page? Yes, we have to do all that. But in doing that,
**00:03:40–00:03:44** we have to ensure that we haven't missed something. And because we've got everyone playing nicely
**00:03:44–00:03:50** in the sandpit, we haven't missed something that's going wrong. So it's critically important
**00:03:50–00:03:55** to take that on board. So when I talk about, I'll say to my staff sometimes, World War
**00:03:55–00:04:00** Z thinking, you've got to think outside the box. What are we missing? What haven't
**00:04:00–00:04:06** we looked at? Now, interestingly, in other environments, particularly my two coaches and
**00:04:06–00:04:13** a coffee podcast with Darren Burgess, I often argue that as sport science practitioners,
**00:04:13–00:04:18** we don't do enough. We're not pushing hard enough. And in not pushing hard enough means
**00:04:18–00:04:22** in some regards, and I see this in many young practitioners, you're expecting current technology
**00:04:22–00:04:27** as the be all and end all. When in fact, most of those technologies, all we're doing
**00:04:27–00:04:33** is inferring an outcome. So we're inferring the athlete can run. We're inferring the athlete
**00:04:33–00:04:37** has recovered, et cetera, et cetera. We're not, in fact, measuring what we say we are.
**00:04:37–00:04:43** That all will start. It's important that we don't get sucked into groupthink. And so
**00:04:43–00:04:48** by I don't think as a practitioner, you should necessarily be going to group. So
**00:04:48–00:04:53** how you go and argue the opposite. I often do it myself. I think it's a leadership thing
**00:04:53–00:04:59** that you should actively think in another path. Now, I have also mentioned in part of
**00:04:59–00:05:04** our module three, we're going to talk about meetings, the kyagi structure and the like.
**00:05:04–00:05:10** One of the critical techniques that I learned, working with a very, very well renowned high
**00:05:10–00:05:14** pressure coach in International Rugby Union, one of the things he used to do was we would
**00:05:14–00:05:20** go into meetings and a subject would come up, it would be discussed, it would be logistics,
**00:05:20–00:05:24** management, perspective, formats, the whole thing. All these different perspectives. And
**00:05:24–00:05:27** you start to come up with something. He would sit quietly, he would say nothing.
**00:05:28–00:05:35** And so then at the end, he would then start to direct questions. But what he was doing
**00:05:35–00:05:41** was thinking in the opposite. And he was thinking like, how do I unravel these things?
**00:05:41–00:05:45** If they can be unraveled by me, they're going to probably be unraveled when we deploy them.
**00:05:45–00:05:52** Equally in situations and the same coach where a subject matter was brought up and no one spoke,
**00:05:52–00:05:56** he would just sit there and wait. He would use the input from all of those different perspectives
**00:05:56–00:06:03** to generate the answer that he felt was most comprehensive. So I quite often will use
**00:06:03–00:06:08** meetings. I may come in with an idea that I might have, this is where I think we need to go. But
**00:06:08–00:06:13** I'll use the people I've got to argue it out. And I'll often turn one against the other to
**00:06:13–00:06:19** try and see what comes out in the mix. So strategically, I'm using that 10th man
**00:06:19–00:06:27** idea in my own head to try and decide if I can break this structure thinking. Have I just got
**00:06:27–00:06:34** stuck down the easy path? Now, another great author, Edward de Bono, he came up with a thing
**00:06:34–00:06:38** or published a book called The Six Hats of Thinking. Now, in The Six Hats of Thinking,
**00:06:38–00:06:44** it's the same thing. It's a structured methodology to consider how we're approaching something. Now,
**00:06:44–00:06:48** in that book, he describes six different colored hats and they represent six different types of
**00:06:48–00:06:54** thinking, emotional, logical, etc, etc. And within that, the idea is that you might designate in a
**00:06:54–00:07:00** meeting, hey, you've got the black hat, you need to think like this, somebody else. I can't say
**00:07:00–00:07:05** that I've ever done that within a meeting. I have done things where I've said to people,
**00:07:05–00:07:09** right, you've got to take the emotion out of this. You're not allowed for the next five minutes,
**00:07:09–00:07:15** you can only speak data. So you can't say we're under pressure from the grand final to get this
**00:07:15–00:07:20** guy right, doesn't matter. Give me the facts. What can we get done by day five? What can we
**00:07:20–00:07:25** get done by day seven? What can we get done by day nine? Can we get them to the game? That type
**00:07:25–00:07:32** thing. Take all the emotion out of it. However, from my own perspective, I will quite regularly
**00:07:32–00:07:38** look in myself and say, right, we've got to think this through logically. We've got to think
**00:07:38–00:07:42** this, take the emotion out of it. I've got to think about this from another perspective.
**00:07:42–00:07:47** What does this look like from the athletes? All that type of thing. But what you're doing
**00:07:47–00:07:54** is developing a manner or a way in which you can approach problems in a more unstructured way.
**00:07:54–00:07:59** So rather than going down, as I said, the group think idea where we get everybody down
**00:07:59–00:08:04** the same path, particularly when we've got repeat problems. When you've got an issue that
**00:08:04–00:08:09** comes back and back again, so where's the problem? We haven't identified it. Now,
**00:08:09–00:08:15** I've unfortunately been in the position where over the course of time I was involved in AFL.
**00:08:16–00:08:20** We're a very, very good team. We're at top of the table, all that sort of thing. We had a run
**00:08:20–00:08:26** of stelitis injuries, all recalcitrant type things. The athlete would finish the game,
**00:08:26–00:08:31** no problem. So we're like, we won, tick it off, move on. But then by Monday, they turn up and
**00:08:31–00:08:37** go, hey, my calf's a bit sore. So we had these insidious onset tears, which were all very small,
**00:08:37–00:08:42** but they were fundamentally fatigue issues. They weren't, they didn't rupture like it's
**00:08:42–00:08:47** blood in any way, shape or form. Through the course of their game and their load,
**00:08:47–00:08:52** that's what was happening. Over and over again, we ended up going down and down the same path.
**00:08:53–00:08:58** Trying to find an answer to that, and certainly one that the coaching group at the time could
**00:08:58–00:09:03** understand or more, not understand, they could intellectually understand it. They had to
**00:09:03–00:09:09** understand it emotionally, particularly the head coach, who although very intelligent would get
**00:09:09–00:09:15** emotional about how things went. So trying to find a solution to that was an amazing process.
**00:09:15–00:09:19** What ended up happening was I had to use the doctor to go to the coach and say,
**00:09:20–00:09:26** just stop, just stop everything. Because at the time, coach wasn't listening to the
**00:09:26–00:09:33** sports science, the analytical component. It was like the doctor going in and giving the devastating
**00:09:33–00:09:39** news of, you have cancer, you have to do this. It was he walked in and just went right,
**00:09:39–00:09:45** you've got to stop, stop, do nothing. Let's take the foot off each other, which we did.
**00:09:45–00:09:48** We went really the other way. We literally stopped training for a period,
**00:09:49–00:09:55** and as that worked out, it drove us into a grand final and went from there. However,
**00:09:55–00:10:00** it was a different approach. We understood the issues, but the approach was different.
**00:10:01–00:10:07** The idea of structured thinking under pressure is about looking at different ways. Now, again,
**00:10:07–00:10:12** when you look at things like this, Daniel Kahneman's book, Thinking Fast, Thinking Slow,
**00:10:12–00:10:19** you look at the two components of how people make decisions. The fast, automatic, intuitive,
**00:10:19–00:10:26** experiential-based, quick, prone to bias type thing, that's the thing. That happens.
**00:10:27–00:10:31** Then we have the smaller, more deliberate analytical, requires effort and attention.
**00:10:31–00:10:38** They're two different things. System 2 can override the errors of System 1,
**00:10:38–00:10:46** but you've got to get past that. Again, it calls into discussion. Can we direct our thinking?
**00:10:47–00:10:51** What's something to put in front of us? Maybe the first thing that we come up with is not
**00:10:51–00:10:56** what we listen to. We need to sit back and look at the most important things,
**00:10:57–00:11:02** and look at the information. What is it? Is there something that needs more time
**00:11:02–00:11:06** to be figured out? This idea of adversarial stress testing,
**00:11:06–00:11:13** pushing ideas, pushing them, pushing yourself to find, have we exhausted everything we've got?
**00:11:13–00:11:21** I think, as a final wrap to this, if you look at the Oodaloop systems that are utilized in the
**00:11:21–00:11:27** military, it's really about orientation in the first place. There's a void in mistake by ensuring
**00:11:27–00:11:33** that we're orientating the way we're focusing in the first place. That's the first part of
**00:11:33–00:11:38** the Oodaloop. There are many ways of thinking in a structured manner, but what you need to ensure
**00:11:38–00:11:44** that is, in that pressured environment of high performance sport, that you get a chance to step
**00:11:44–00:11:50** away. You must make time. You cannot be working in the business all the time. You need to work on
**00:11:50–00:11:57** the business. As a leader, on the business component is how you address the system.
**00:11:57–00:12:06** We talked about, in the final component of Module 6, VLAB 6.8, I talked about don't let things be
**00:12:06–00:12:12** set and forget. Let's say we're building that system between the performance and medical stuff.
**00:12:12–00:12:19** Once you've built one that's working, you need to keep reassessing it. You can't just let it go
**00:12:19–00:12:23** and say, it's going to burn forever, because you're going to have different people come in
**00:12:23–00:12:27** and out of that. You might have people start to evolve their ideas. You might have a young
**00:12:27–00:12:32** practitioner in S&C enrolled in the first place, but after a year or so, he starts to develop new
**00:12:32–00:12:39** ideas. That does happen. People change. Equally, technology changes. Information changes. We get
**00:12:39–00:12:44** more information. We know more about a situation now, two years later, than we might have done
**00:12:44–00:12:50** previously. There's a lot of different moving paths. The point to all of that is ensuring
**00:12:50–00:12:57** that, as a leader, you do take a step back. You do put your time into the business, but you work
**00:12:57–00:13:02** on the business by stepping away and reviewing. Reviewing all the parts, but as a central thing,
**00:13:02–00:13:09** as crass as it may sound, answering the question, what will suck this up? What will unravel me?
**00:13:09–00:13:13** This is all working really well. What will mess it up? If you can do that,
**00:13:13–00:13:20** and whether it's by the tent man rule, or the bono's detached, or whatever it is,
**00:13:20–00:13:26** you need to come up with a methodology that ensures that you approach those problems regularly,
**00:13:26–00:13:31** because they can become problems. What seems nice and stable and everything's cool,
**00:13:31–00:13:36** at the moment, may unravel at the point when you don't need it to. Staying on top of that is a
**00:13:36–00:13:42** critical part of leadership. In any case, I recommend going to watch World War Z and
**00:13:42–00:13:47** understand that while it's a little bit dramatized, it is actually real. That's how we
**00:13:47–00:13:58** produce structured thinking under pressure.

=== PAGE 1 ===
OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  Podcast Reference Document 
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  obpacademy.com 
Page 
STRUCTURED THINKING UNDER PRESSURE 
The Science of Avoiding Blind Spots 
OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  –  Podcast Reference Document
THE PROBLEM: YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT YOU'RE MISSING 
In 1973, Israel's military intelligence missed one of the most consequential attacks in modern history. The 
Yom Kippur War caught them by surprise — not because the information wasn't available, but because 
every analyst who looked at that information reached the same conclusion: Egypt won't attack. Nine out 
of ten. Maybe ten out of ten. 
That is not an intelligence failure. That is a thinking failure. And it happens in performance departments 
every week. 
This document synthesises the key frameworks from leadership and cognitive science that address this 
single problem: how do you structure your thinking — and your team's thinking — so that you catch what 
consensus hides? Each framework is real, has a documented history, and has direct application to how 
performance leaders make decisions. Together they form the basis of the OBP Bias Prompt Analysis 
protocol used in the SpeedSig Primer Course. 
THE OBP CONNECTION
In the Structured Thinking Under Pressure Podcast the idea of challenging group-thinking is presented  
using the movie World War Z as a starting point. This document provides the intellectual scaffolding 
behind that podcast — and shows how it connects to the broader decision architecture running through 
OBP's Go/No-Go framework, Kaigi Meeting Discipline, and the Knowledge–Behaviour Matrix.
1. THE 10TH MAN RULE — DEVIL'S ADVOCACY AS DISCIPLINE 
Is it real? 
The World War Z film (2013) portrays Israel as having institutionalised a rule: if nine leaders reach the 
same conclusion from the same information, it is the formal obligation of the tenth to disagree. The movie 
frames this as the reason Israel built a wall against the zombie outbreak. 
The Hollywood version is dramatized — but the underlying institution is real. Following the Agranat 
Commission inquiry into the 1973 Yom Kippur War, Israeli Military Intelligence established what is 
formally known as the Devil's Advocate Unit (Hebrew: Makhleket HaBakara — "the comptroller 
department"). It operates independently within the Research Department, reports directly to the Director 
of Military Intelligence, and its sole purpose is to examine unlikely scenarios and challenge prevailing 
assumptions. 
=== PAGE 2 ===
OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  Podcast Reference Document 
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  obpacademy.com 
Page 
HISTORICAL RECORD
The Agranat Commission found that Israeli intelligence had fallen victim to what analysts call 'the concept' 
— a locked-in interpretive framework that filtered out contradicting evidence. The Devil's Advocate Unit 
was the structural response. It was not a suggestion that someone play devil's advocate. It was a 
permanent role with institutional authority.
Why consensus is the enemy 
The 10th Man Rule targets a specific and well-documented failure mode: groupthink. Psychologist Irving 
Janis documented the phenomenon in 1982, observing that cohesive groups under pressure develop a 
bias toward harmony that actively suppresses dissent. The more trust and esprit de corps in a group, the 
higher the risk that critical thinking will be replaced by collective rationalisation. 
This is not disloyalty. It is physics. When a group shares common training, common experience, and 
common language, they share common blind spots. Consensus becomes a false signal of correctness. 
The 10th Man principle corrects for this not by creating conflict — but by creating a formal, expected, 
protected role for the contrarian view. 
THE PRACTITIONER TRANSLATION
In your department: when your whole staff team agrees that an athlete is ready to return, or that a 
monitoring metric looks fine, or that the program is working — that's exactly when you need someone 
whose job it is to ask: what if we're all wrong? Not to create chaos. To stress-test the consensus before it 
costs you.
2. DE BONO'S SIX THINKING HATS — STRUCTURED PERSPECTIVE 
ROTATION 
Edward de Bono's Six Thinking Hats (1985) addresses a related but distinct problem. Where the 10th 
Man corrects for consensus after it forms, de Bono's system prevents premature consensus by 
structuring the thinking process itself. Rather than letting a group free-form through a decision — where 
dominant voices, status hierarchies, and emotional reactions determine what gets explored — the Six 
Hats assigns every participant a thinking mode simultaneously. 
The Six Hats 
Hat
Mode
Sport Performance Application
White Hat
Facts & Data Only
What does the monitoring data actually say? Strip out interpretation 
— just the numbers, the observations, the objective record.
Red Hat
Emotions & Gut Feeling
What is your gut telling you about this athlete's readiness? What are 
coaches instinctively reacting to? Say it without justification.
Black Hat
Critical / Caution
What could go wrong with this RTR decision? What are the risk 
factors we might be underweighting? (The 10th Man hat.)
=== PAGE 3 ===
OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  Podcast Reference Document 
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  obpacademy.com 
Page 
Yellow Hat
Optimism / Benefits
What is the best case here? What does successful return look like? 
What is working in the athlete's favour?
Green Hat
Creativity / Alternatives
Is there a different path we haven't considered? A modified training 
load? A staged return we haven't designed yet?
Blue Hat
Process Control
Are we having the right conversation? Have we used all the hats? 
Who owns the decision, and what is the review trigger?
De Bono's key insight is that parallel thinking — everyone in the same mode at the same time — is more 
productive and less conflictual than oppositional thinking. You're not arguing black against yellow. You 
are all wearing the black hat at the same time. The conflict disappears; the thinking remains. 
3. THE PRE-MORTEM — IMAGINING FAILURE BEFORE IT HAPPENS 
Gary Klein introduced the pre-mortem as a formal technique in the late 1990s, subsequently popularised 
by Daniel Kahneman in Thinking, Fast and Slow. The mechanism is deliberately counterintuitive: before 
committing to a decision, the group assumes the decision has already been made and has already failed. 
The question shifts from 'could this fail?' to 'it failed — now, why?' 
This framing is critical. When you ask 'could this fail?' in a group that has just spent 20 minutes building 
consensus around a plan, the social pressure to protect that consensus suppresses honest risk 
identification. When you assume the failure has already occurred, that pressure evaporates. People have 
permission to identify problems — even the ones they were too polite to raise during planning. 
MCKINSEY ON PRE-MORTEMS
McKinsey's organisational decision research identifies the pre-mortem as one of the most consistently 
effective interventions for countering groupthink in executive decision-making. The key is that the structure 
of the exercise makes it safe to identify problems — because the group is no longer defending a plan, 
they are diagnosing a failure.
Pre-Mortem: The Three-Step Protocol 
1. State the decision clearly — what has been decided? 
2. Project forward 6–12 months and state: "It is [date]. The decision failed. What happened?" Each 
person writes independently before discussion. 
3. Collect all failure scenarios. Group them. Use the most credible ones to stress-test the plan or 
add contingencies before committing. 
IN YOUR DEPARTMENT
You have signed off on a return-to-play timeline. Before the athlete goes back on the field, ask your team: 
'It's four weeks from now. He's reinjured. What happened?' The answers that emerge — the things nobody 
said in the planning meeting — are the real risks. That is where your contingency planning should focus.
=== PAGE 4 ===
OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  Podcast Reference Document 
© OLDBULL PERFORMANCE  |  obpacademy.com 
Page 
4. KAHNEMAN'S SYSTEM 1 & SYSTEM 2 — FAST AND SLOW THINKING 
Daniel Kahneman's Nobel Prize-winning work frames all human cognition as operating through two 
systems. System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive, and pattern-based — it is your experienced practitioner 
reading the room and knowing something is off before they can explain why. System 2 is slow, deliberate, 
analytical, and effortful — it is your structured review process, your data analysis, your decision log. 
Neither system is superior. System 1 is essential: under time pressure and in high-familiarity 
environments, the fast-thinking heuristics of experienced practitioners are genuinely valuable. The 
problem arises when System 1 operates in high-stakes, novel, or complex scenarios — particularly when 
the situation looks familiar but isn't. System 1 cannot tell the difference between pattern-matching and 
pattern-confabulation. 
System 1 — Fast
System 2 — Slow
Automatic & intuitive
Deliberate & analytical
Pattern recognition from experience
Logical reasoning from evidence
Operates below conscious awareness
Requires effort and attention
Prone to confirmation bias
Can override System 1 errors
Ideal for routine calls
Required for novel/high-stakes decisions

What is working in the athlete's favour?
Green Hat
Creativity / Alternatives
Is there a different path we haven't considered? A modified training 
load? A staged return we haven't designed yet?
Blue Hat
Process Control
Are we having the right conversation? Have we used all the hats? 
Who owns the decision, and what is the review trigger?
De Bono's key insight is that parallel thinking — everyone in the same mode at the same time — is more 
productive and less conflictual than oppositional thinking. You're not arguing black against yellow. You 
are all wearing the black hat at the same time. The conflict disappears; the thinking remains. 
3. THE PRE-MORTEM — IMAGINING FAILURE BEFORE IT HAPPENS 
Gary Klein introduced the pre-mortem as a formal technique in the late 1990s, subsequently popularised 
by Daniel Kahneman in Thinking, Fast and Slow. The mechanism is deliberately counterintuitive: before 
committing to a decision, the group assumes the decision has already been made and has already failed. 
The question shifts from 'could this fail?' to 'it failed — now, why?' 
This framing is critical. When you ask 'could this fail?' in a group that has just spent 20 minutes building 
consensus around a plan, the social pressure to protect that consensus suppresses honest risk 
identification. When you assume the failure has already occurred, that pressure evaporates. People have 
permission to identify problems — even the ones they were too polite to raise during planning. 
MCKINSEY ON PRE-MORTEMS
McKinsey's organisational decision research identifies the pre-mortem as one of the most consistently 
effective interventions for countering groupthink in executive decision-making. The key is that the structure 
of the exercise makes it safe to identify problems — because the group is no longer defending a plan, 
they are diagnosing a failure.
Pre-Mortem: The Three-Step Protocol 
1. State the decision clearly — what has been decided? 
2. Project forward 6–12 months and state: "It is [date]. The decision failed. What happened?" Each 
person writes independently before discussion. 
3. Collect all failure scenarios. Group them. Use the most credible ones to stress-test the plan or 
add contingencies before committing. 
IN YOUR DEPARTMENT
You have signed off on a return-to-play timeline. Before the athlete goes back on the field, ask your team: 
'It's four weeks from now. He's reinjured. What happened?' The answers that emerge — the things nobody 
said in the planning meeting — are the real risks. That is where your contingency planning should focus.
=== PAGE 4 ===

Page 
4. KAHNEMAN'S SYSTEM 1 & SYSTEM 2 — FAST AND SLOW THINKING 
Daniel Kahneman's Nobel Prize-winning work frames all human cognition as operating through two 
systems. System 1 is fast, automatic, intuitive, and pattern-based — it is your experienced practitioner 
reading the room and knowing something is off before they can explain why. System 2 is slow, deliberate, 
analytical, and effortful — it is your structured review process, your data analysis, your decision log. 
Neither system is superior. System 1 is essential: under time pressure and in high-familiarity 
environments, the fast-thinking heuristics of experienced practitioners are genuinely valuable. The 
problem arises when System 1 operates in high-stakes, novel, or complex scenarios — particularly when 
the situation looks familiar but isn't. System 1 cannot tell the difference between pattern-matching and 
pattern-confabulation. 
System 1 — Fast
System 2 — Slow
Automatic & intuitive
Deliberate & analytical
Pattern recognition from experience
Logical reasoning from evidence
Operates below conscious awareness
Requires effort and attention
Prone to confirmation bias
Can override System 1 errors
Ideal for routine calls
Required for novel/high-stakes decisions

Source: downloaded Podcast 3 audio, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. Examples and research claims below are attributed to the speaker, not independently checked.
## Main idea
The speaker argues that recurring operational decision meetings should be tightly prepared and time-limited. Saving meeting time protects staff capacity for analysis, project work, and work around training and treatment schedules. His “20 minutes” is a target for suitable routine meetings, not a limit he applies to every discussion. (00:00–01:28; 02:58–04:24; 05:24–06:19; 09:39–09:51)
## Meeting structure
1. Send information in advance, ideally about 24 hours before, so attendees can read and consider it. State the required outcome at the start. (07:20–08:16)
2. Keep the discussion on what is working, what is not, and what needs to change. Give creative or exploratory work its own meeting format. (08:16–08:34; 14:10–14:42)
3. Name who will decide when a decision is needed. End with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update. (08:34–09:39)
4. Start and end on time. Use a visible timer where it helps, and put useful off-topic issues in a “parking lot” with an owner and next step. (10:08–11:11)
The speaker gives an example of a facilitator using short timed rounds to collect responses to three questions from five people. That planning meeting lasted about 40 minutes and, in his view, prepared months of work. He also cites short daily stand-ups as a way to surface completed work, next work, and blockers. (01:28–02:58; 11:11–11:26)
## Limits and next step
For complex problems, the speaker suggests preparation, smaller pieces, and small multidisciplinary groups. He explicitly distinguishes brainstorming and relationship-building from a short decision meeting. His challenge is to tighten **one** recurring meeting, then ask whether anything valuable was lost and whether its outputs improved. (12:16–15:31; 16:10–16:44)

## Main idea
The speaker argues that recurring operational decision meetings should be tightly prepared and time-limited. 1. Send information in advance, ideally about 24 hours before, so attendees can read and consider it. State the required outcome at the start. (07:20–08:16)
2. Keep the discussion on what is working, what is not, and what needs to change. Give creative or exploratory work its own meeting format. (08:16–08:34; 14:10–14:42)
3. Name who will decide when a decision is needed. End with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update. (08:34–09:39)
4. Start and end on time. Use a visible timer where it helps, and put useful off-topic issues in a “parking lot” with an owner and next step. (10:08–11:11)
The speaker gives an example of a facilitator using short timed rounds to collect responses to three questions from five people. That planning meeting lasted about 40 minutes and, in his view, prepared months of work. He also cites short daily stand-ups as a way to surface completed work, next work, and blockers. For complex problems, the speaker suggests preparation, smaller pieces, and small multidisciplinary groups. He explicitly distinguishes brainstorming and relationship-building from a short decision meeting. His challenge is to tighten **one** recurring meeting, then ask whether anything valuable was lost and whether its outputs improved. (12:16–15:31; 16:10–16:44)

#### I
Source: downloaded Part I video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft; neuroscience and performance claims are presented as the speaker's account.
## Main idea
The speaker argues that predictable communication, clear roles, and established operating routines reduce the time leaders spend interpreting routine requests. He frames that saved attention as capacity for planning and handling difficult problems. (00:00–00:59; 02:52–05:05)
## Examples
- A head coach, doctor, and strength coach may all ask about “training load,” yet each is asking from a different concern and level of technical knowledge. The leader needs shared language and an understanding of each person's context to respond efficiently. (00:59–02:46)
- The speaker uses a military analogy, with an explicit warning that military and sport stakes differ: rehearsed fundamentals allow a team to act without inventing a process during a pressured moment. For a performance department, he applies that idea chiefly to communication routines. (05:05–07:04)
- In one AFL example, the coach and performance staff knew their drills and exposure measures well enough to change a session during play and estimate the consequences for specific players. The speaker credits prior planning and a shared technical language for that flexibility. (07:05–09:03)
## Operational implication
As departments grow, the speaker sees ambiguity, interruptions, and coordination among more staff as demands on a leader's attention. He recommends defining responsibilities and common communication rules so routine work is predictable and changes can be made deliberately. This is an argument drawn from his examples, not an independently tested effect in this summary. (09:03–11:30)
#### II
Source: downloaded Part II video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft. This summary reports the speaker's practices; claims about cognitive effects and communication methods are not independently validated.
## Main idea
The speaker names five operating practices: develop a common language, define communication mechanisms, document operating procedures, lead by strategic intent, and give clear feedback. This part concentrates on common language and communication expectations. (00:00–01:09)
## Common language
The speaker recommends replacing technical language with terms the audience already uses, without losing the link to measurement. In one AFL example, he and a coach agreed on verbal running categories, then used those categories in reporting rather than leading with speed units. He recommends explaining processes in plain terms, documenting them where useful, offering coaches short reference sheets, and learning their preferred words and report format early in the season. (01:09–06:11)
## Communication rules
- Specify which channel carries each kind of information and what behavior is expected. For injuries, explain in advance when the coach will receive a provisional update and when a more specific medical update may be available. (06:11–07:48)
- Agree on the timing and form of post-training reports. The speaker describes different coaches who preferred very different amounts and formats of information. (07:48–08:39)
- Mark messages by urgency or purpose, and make meeting invitations explicit about objective, length, and preparation. Project assignments should state the deliverable, deadline, expected quality, and people to consult. Set expectations for response times as well. (08:39–10:09)
**Practical takeaway:** Agree on terms, reporting formats, channels, and update timing before pressure rises, so staff know what information to provide and where to find it.
#### III
Source: downloaded Part III video, transcribed locally with faster-whisper. Timestamps refer to the media. The transcript is a machine-generated, unverified draft; this summary presents the speaker's management approach rather than tested outcomes.
## Main idea
The speaker finishes his “discipline creates freedom” argument with three practices: document repeatable procedures, give staff a clear strategic direction with defined decision boundaries, and provide direct, regular feedback. He argues that these practices reduce ambiguity and give both leaders and staff more room for focused work. (00:00–00:38; 03:56–07:18; 07:18–09:15)
## Operating practices
- **Document routine work.** Specify who handles equipment, session preparation, data collection, testing, and other recurring tasks. Review procedures when they need improvement. The speaker wants leaders to provide oversight while staff know their day-to-day responsibilities. (00:00–02:12)
- **Remove avoidable ambiguity.** Explain the purpose of a meeting request, set clear deadlines, and state each person's role. The speaker says vague requests leave staff guessing and consume attention. (02:12–03:17)
- **Set direction and decision limits.** He uses a highway analogy: the leader names the destination and boundaries, while staff choose tactics within them. He would give an experienced colleague more discretion than a new hire and make clear which decisions must be escalated. (03:56–06:30)
- **Make time for feedback.** Schedule check-ins, address performance issues promptly and clearly, document consequential discussions, and ask staff for feedback on one's own leadership. (07:18–09:15)
**Practical takeaway:** Define the work and its boundaries well enough that staff can act without constant permission, then use regular feedback to refine the system. (09:15–11:11)

**00:00:20–00:00:26** theme of this webinar. We know it can generate reduced mental overheads because of constant
**00:00:26–00:00:32** coordination is reduced and we create space and that space we play replaced with creativity,
**00:00:32–00:00:39** curiosity, deep thinking, all the things that will separate you as a leadership professional inside of
**00:00:39–00:00:45** pro sport. So that answer, as I said, is very boring. There are five things we need to work
**00:00:45–00:00:50** through. We need to develop a common language, create communication mechanisms, build an operational
**00:00:50–00:00:56** procedures list, lead by strategic intent and provide clear and honest feedback. This is
**00:00:56–00:01:04** fundamentally a basic overview of how you run your leadership group and how you operate within your
**00:01:04–00:01:09** staff. So developing a common language. Every domain has its own vocabulary, priorities, communication
**00:01:09–00:01:16** norms, etc. If we don't have a common language, then communication becomes translation. And that
**00:01:16–00:01:21** means that we have to actively think about what we're saying and how we're saying it. Think about
**00:01:21–00:01:27** working in another language. I think in English, I have to translate it to Spanish, I have to speak
**00:01:27–00:01:33** about it in Spanish, hear the answer back in Spanish, decode it back to English to think about
**00:01:33–00:01:38** it. That's a lot of work. And if you're doing the same thing, trying to communicate complex
**00:01:40–00:01:44** concepts and the like to coaches, staff, whatever, it's really important that you
**00:01:44–00:01:50** understand that that mental cost will be high. Now be very clear, this common language is in all
**00:01:50–00:01:55** directions. You're managing it up to the people you're reporting to, coaches, board members, whatever
**00:01:55–00:02:00** it is, lateral to your other department managers, and then down to your staff. Trying to get this
**00:02:00–00:02:06** organized so that operationally you can reduce this cost because the translation cost goes down.
**00:02:08–00:02:13** What are the key parts to developing a common language? Number one, by far the biggest is
**00:02:13–00:02:22** demystify. Don't be that tool that tries to use big sports science, language, statistics, whatever,
**00:02:22–00:02:31** two people that don't need to hear it. I famously, we used to work in my AFL, one of the stories I
**00:02:31–00:02:37** said called, one of the stories I relayed earlier, in the same area, we didn't talk about speed zones
**00:02:37–00:02:43** and running. We had verbal anchors for everything. So there was a jog, there was a stride, there was
**00:02:43–00:02:50** a sprint, there was a gut run. There were things that now gut run outside AFL will mean nothing.
**00:02:50–00:02:53** If you're listening in the US or Europe, you will not understand what gut run is,
**00:02:53–00:03:00** but it's a very, very strong component in AFL football that coaches understand. So I remember
**00:03:00–00:03:05** standing on the field and going, coach, describe that. You can see the player running through the
**00:03:05–00:03:11** field. He goes, that's a gut run. I'm like, good on, good on you. We've got it. So we can
**00:03:11–00:03:16** measure that. Therefore, when we discussed, we talked about gut run. When I reported,
**00:03:16–00:03:22** I didn't report in meters per second or kilometers per hour, I reported in those anchors. So
**00:03:22–00:03:26** demystifying terms to make it easy for the person who you're communicating to.
**00:03:26–00:03:31** From a process perspective, explain what, why, how you do things in simple terms. Some of it
**00:03:31–00:03:36** may even be worthwhile documenting within a procedures manual. When you're looking at
**00:03:36–00:03:41** staff you're working with, explaining what, why, how you do things is really important.
**00:03:41–00:03:46** A key variable that is very much a part of leadership role in a sporting environment
**00:03:46–00:03:51** is working with your media department. Now your media department are another whole set of people.
**00:03:51–00:03:55** They're not going to understand necessarily anything you do. Working with that and making
**00:03:55–00:03:59** sure you get those folks lined up with what are the things you want and don't want.
**00:03:59–00:04:04** I used to always, I've been very clear with my media partner whenever I've gone,
**00:04:04–00:04:08** we can video certain things. You're going to want to ask me permission before you do anything,
**00:04:08–00:04:14** but we're never going to get in the line of a player's sight. Put a lens on, step back,
**00:04:14–00:04:18** get out of the way. You're not going to be upfront in that person's eyes.
**00:04:18–00:04:22** So when the media department come down, they know what they're expecting from me.
**00:04:22–00:04:27** I'm trying to try and help them out and get, as they say, color for the media,
**00:04:27–00:04:33** but we're going to control that environment to the level of discipline that I require.
**00:04:33–00:04:38** Once you've explained that, it's really easy for them to operate. Again, it reduces that load.
**00:04:39–00:04:45** I love the idea of cheat sheets, particularly with all the monitoring and testing, critical processes
**00:04:45–00:04:49** that you might go through with coaching stuff in particular. Give them a cheat sheet.
**00:04:49–00:04:55** Show them, make it easy. Coaches, when we talk about football, this is how we'll discuss it.
**00:04:55–00:04:59** But do it early in the season before everything gets started. There is nothing
**00:04:59–00:05:05** more debilitating than in the middle of a season when coaches are under pressure and you introduce
**00:05:05–00:05:10** a new variable and go, hey, we're going to now measure this thing and it's too hard, too hard by
**00:05:10–00:05:15** far. Making sure you get those things squared away early is absolutely critical.
**00:05:15–00:05:20** Now, this last point, critical point, I will say that listening and adapting to what coaching
**00:05:20–00:05:28** staff say in the vernacular they use is incredibly important. Ask a coach how they
**00:05:28–00:05:34** communicate. Listen and use it. If a coach says, I like to see things in tables, don't give him a
**00:05:34–00:05:40** graph. No matter how pretty it is, doesn't matter. Give him what he wants or she, give them what they
**00:05:40–00:05:45** want. Now, if you dig into the topic of neuro-linguistic programming, one of the key elements
**00:05:45–00:05:50** they talk about that is to gain people's confidence, is to listen to how they speak
**00:05:50–00:05:55** and speak back to them in the same manner so that they're hearing a comforting voice.
**00:05:55–00:06:00** A coach hearing their language back promotes confidence and that's what you need. You need
**00:06:00–00:06:06** to be successful by having a coach understand you. Listening intently, making sure it's
**00:06:06–00:06:11** detailed and working towards that common language. Now, your communication mechanisms.
**00:06:11–00:06:15** This has gotten, communications got more complicated as time's gone because we now
**00:06:15–00:06:21** have more vehicles. Yes, we have to face to face, but we have the social media apps, we have
**00:06:22–00:06:29** emails, we have loops, we have all these little bits and pieces, which in a complicated
**00:06:29–00:06:34** environment, if we don't discuss those and get them down pat, they're a pain in the butt.
**00:06:34–00:06:39** Absolutely. You want to state clearly what's acceptable and what's not. That's more from a,
**00:06:39–00:06:44** this is how we're like the standards of actual communication, but when we talk about channels,
**00:06:44–00:06:48** we want to be sure this is what we're going to do. When we talk about this meeting,
**00:06:48–00:06:53** the information will be in this channel. When you get to very specific things like post injuries,
**00:06:53–00:06:58** a big one, I would always say to my coach, hey, if we get an injury, this is how it's going to
**00:06:58–00:07:02** roll a big one. We're going to get the athlete off the field and we're going to make them safe.
**00:07:02–00:07:08** Number one, we're going to get an idea. If the guy's come off and he's legs like that,
**00:07:08–00:07:13** we know it's fractured. It's a big deal. You'll get that information, but a lot of times an
**00:07:13–00:07:17** athlete will come off the field and you won't really know how bad it is. We're going to go for
**00:07:17–00:07:21** scans a lot, but having the coach understand what the tempo of that information is.
**00:07:21–00:07:25** Coach, we're going to finish the game. You'll do your normal talk to the players as you do.
**00:07:25–00:07:29** I will come in after that meeting and I will give you our best estimate of where we're at,
**00:07:29–00:07:33** what we're dealing with, but I'm not going to be able to give you anything specific.
**00:07:33–00:07:38** Once that happens, we know that next morning we're going to get that scanned and the
**00:07:38–00:07:43** doctor will speak to you the next morning and we'll go from there, but having that clarity,
**00:07:43–00:07:48** so coach is not going searching for it. Post training reports, same thing.
**00:07:48–00:07:53** This day and age, there's so many ways to do it. I used to work with my short time in football,
**00:07:53–00:07:59** in the world game, working with GPS systems that went to a tablet. I was able to finish
**00:07:59–00:08:03** the session. Players were coming off. The units were being collected, but we were already
**00:08:03–00:08:10** downloading. We could put a very simple session report to PDF into the coach. He was already on
**00:08:10–00:08:17** it. I had another coach many years ago who from a testing perspective, he just liked to see volume
**00:08:17–00:08:23** fundamentally. I wrote code back in the late 90s that was able to take our data and produce
**00:08:23–00:08:28** multiple reports. He'd get a book that thick with all the data in it. That's what he felt.
**00:08:28–00:08:34** Having that weight of information, that's what he needed. We delivered it to give them
**00:08:34–00:08:39** confidence that what they've got is what they need. When you're triaging designations around
**00:08:41–00:08:48** messaging, particularly emails, is urgent routine, just FYI, accession, getting people to put those
**00:08:48–00:08:55** on so we know where it's at. Then, as we've discussed in other mediums, that meeting discipline,
**00:08:55–00:09:00** really knowing the type, the purpose, the structure. Again, that's another conversation
**00:09:00–00:09:06** elsewhere. What happens with comms is we get clear expectations. We get roles and responsibilities.
**00:09:06–00:09:12** Having your staff really know what they're doing and what their jobs are is critical,
**00:09:12–00:09:17** particularly when it even comes to small things like training, ensuring that everybody has a role
**00:09:17–00:09:21** and they know where it is. If people get lost around that, it really drives frustration
**00:09:22–00:09:28** in staff and that can unravel people. Again, it becomes another spot fire that you have to
**00:09:28–00:09:34** put out. Make sure your meeting invitations have got clear objective duration, required prep,
**00:09:34–00:09:39** because when people don't have that, it becomes stressful. Same with project assignments,
**00:09:39–00:09:45** specified deliverable, deadline, quality, who consult, et cetera. Making sure you've
**00:09:45–00:09:51** got that down pat helps people understand where they're at. Make sure everything's got a clear
**00:09:51–00:09:58** purpose. As I said before, we've got new vehicles, Slack, et cetera, for coordination.
**00:09:58–00:10:03** You want to make sure people know where that is. The last one is really that response time,
**00:10:03–00:10:09** making sure that everybody understands what is expected. When should an email be answered?

**00:00:21–00:00:27** there's no mystical skill here. The art of controlling time is really about how we structure
**00:00:27–00:00:32** our world around us in a performance department in order to effectively control our time.
**00:00:32–00:00:38** So, our aims in this webinar will be to understand the neuroscience that underpins executive function.
**00:00:38–00:00:43** Now we'll explain executive function, but our executive function fundamentally determines
**00:00:43–00:00:48** how effective you are as a leader. We're going to look at recognizing the hidden sources of cognitive
**00:00:48–00:00:53** load. We're going to provide a logic to systemize the fundamentals, and we're going to provide
**00:00:53–00:00:59** concrete implementation strategies to control your time. So here's the challenge. In the space of a
**00:00:59–00:01:04** very short period of time, you could be confronted with a head coach saying, I want to talk to you
**00:01:04–00:01:09** about training load. Then less than a couple of heartbeaks, it can be the senior doctor saying,
**00:01:09–00:01:14** I want to talk to you about training load. Then your SNC coach, I want to talk to you about
**00:01:14–00:01:20** training load. So we've got the same question, three different people. Those questions are,
**00:01:20–00:01:26** although the same sentence structure, they're all different questions based on the perspective
**00:01:26–00:01:32** of the individual, where they're coming from as a practitioner, a medical head coach, the SNC coach,
**00:01:32–00:01:37** the context. SNC coach may be working on some planning going forward and want to understand
**00:01:37–00:01:42** where the load's at and what we're expecting to do. Coach may be concerned that the players
**00:01:42–00:01:46** are looking flat on the field. Doctor may be concerned with what she believes is an
**00:01:46–00:01:51** injury trend. So it's vastly different the information contained in his question,
**00:01:51–00:01:57** not to mention the knowledge. The knowledge base of those three professionals is enormously
**00:01:57–00:02:03** different. The head coach, for as smart as he may be, may not know a whole lot about training
**00:02:03–00:02:08** exposure measures and game exposure measures. Therefore, your ability to interact with him
**00:02:08–00:02:14** will be predicated on the type of information you can convey. The SNC coach should have
**00:02:14–00:02:19** a comparable knowledge to yourself. A doctor, a game, eminently professional in their own
**00:02:19–00:02:26** environment, but typically doctors don't generally understand the relationship of training and
**00:02:27–00:02:32** particular variables to the outcome on the field. They're going to have an insight, but it's going
**00:02:32–00:02:37** to be different. Not the least to which the last point is experience. All of those three people
**00:02:37–00:02:42** may be in their first year of the job, which puts a vastly different spin
**00:02:42–00:02:46** again on that same question. So how are you going? How's your first couple of minutes of
**00:02:46–00:02:52** work been when you've been confronted by this? So let's have a quick look at the neuroscience.
**00:02:52–00:02:57** Your brain has limited executive function capacity. Executive function capacity is your
**00:02:57–00:03:06** brain's ability to recognize patterns, to recognize patterns, to deal with complex
**00:03:06–00:03:11** problems. And what that means is that every decision, every ambiguous situation,
**00:03:11–00:03:17** every coordination task depletes this resource. What I just showed you, that challenge, is a
**00:03:17–00:03:23** coordination task because you're having to chop and change between where people are, what they
**00:03:23–00:03:29** understand in the context perspective. But when your systems are disciplined and predictable,
**00:03:29–00:03:34** routine operations become automatic. So a question like that about load, if you've
**00:03:35–00:03:39** managed your environment, if you've worked on getting your staff around you, not just your
**00:03:39–00:03:45** staff, but the staff you communicate to, set up to the point that you can have good,
**00:03:45–00:03:50** solid, quick conversations. You understand the context, you understand their education,
**00:03:50–00:03:57** they understand you. That is incredibly important because this frees your prefrontal cortex for
**00:03:57–00:04:02** higher order thinking, which is this is your executive function, strategy, innovation, pattern
**00:04:02–00:04:08** recognition, complex problem solving. So what we can conclude from this is that we know there is
**00:04:08–00:04:12** a limited capacity. And I can tell you from experience that when you're dealing with
**00:04:12–00:04:19** this sort of stuff every day, day and out, what people might call putting out spot fires. You
**00:04:19–00:04:23** speak to someone, how's your day going? I'm just putting out lots of spot fires. Well,
**00:04:23–00:04:28** they're dealing with lots and lots of little pieces. This is draining. And this can really
**00:04:28–00:04:32** distract from the job that you need to do. So as a leader, particularly a high performance
**00:04:32–00:04:37** manager leader, someone who's managing a complex department, not just performance department,
**00:04:37–00:04:40** although this can apply to that, but something where you're involved with multiple domains,
**00:04:40–00:04:46** you've got medical, you might have psychology, dietetics, all of those pieces,
**00:04:46–00:04:53** along with performance in that same puzzle. Getting those people on side and in a coordinated
**00:04:53–00:05:00** manner so your communication can be very direct and very manageable is incredibly important to your
**00:05:00–00:05:05** survival. So the paradox of discipline. This has been written about extensively by a guy
**00:05:05–00:05:10** named Jocko Willnick. So he's an ex Navy SEALs commander. Now, I'm not in the habit
**00:05:11–00:05:19** of utilizing military stories as some sort of equal to sport. They've got no direct relationship
**00:05:19–00:05:24** whatsoever. And the context in which military is applied is far beyond anything that would be
**00:05:24–00:05:30** experienced in sport. The lessons that we can learn from people who've been in that environment
**00:05:30–00:05:36** at that extreme level, we can bring that back. Now, Jocko Willnick talks about his core thesis
**00:05:36–00:05:42** is extreme ownership, this rigid discipline in fundamentals that allows space to adapt and
**00:05:42–00:05:48** innovate under pressure. So he says no debate on protocols. So the idea is when you consider
**00:05:48–00:05:54** a military environment, they will have drills for certain situations. So if they're in a laneway
**00:05:54–00:05:58** and they're having to tactically withdraw because there's a force coming at them,
**00:05:58–00:06:03** they will do it in a certain manner. One will lay down fire, they'll bunny hop around and
**00:06:03–00:06:08** they'll continue to support each other doing that. And I'm just relaying a story there. However,
**00:06:08–00:06:13** they do that task in a particular manner. Understanding that when as a Navy SEAL
**00:06:13–00:06:20** commander, Jocko might have called a tactical retreat that his soldiers know exactly what to
**00:06:20–00:06:27** do, which means he's got this free colony bandwidth to work on tactical chaos in that drama.
**00:06:27–00:06:32** Now, we're not necessarily always talking about chaos, but unquestionably, sports environments
**00:06:32–00:06:39** get to a very, very chaotic position at certain times. The more we can understand what this
**00:06:39–00:06:44** discipline in fundamentals looks like, and the case would be the example used from the outset,
**00:06:44–00:06:49** it's really communication. It's getting communication fundamentals down so that once
**00:06:49–00:06:54** you are under pressure, you've got control. You don't have to be recreating the wheel
**00:06:54–00:06:59** every single time you have a conversation. This is a great example of how the paradox
**00:06:59–00:07:04** of discipline is effective. Now, we'll take that a little bit further.
**00:07:05–00:07:10** Before we go into this slide, we'll talk about what I would say is I had a coach I worked with
**00:07:10–00:07:16** where he was adamant about the idea that we would be nimble. He would always say,
**00:07:16–00:07:19** we've got to be nimble, we've got to be nimble. But in fact, when he worked with me,
**00:07:19–00:07:24** certainly in planning training sessions, he was by far one of the best I've ever worked with.
**00:07:24–00:07:31** He knew our drills. We had the metrics down that we were sharing across the domain, and we were able
**00:07:31–00:07:38** to plan. I could walk in and say, boss, we've got X amount of volume for today. We want to do some
**00:07:38–00:07:43** certain amount of contact. He would go, I want to do this drill, so we know that drill X time.
**00:07:44–00:07:48** He'd be able to space out his drills. In fact, prior to recording this today,
**00:07:48–00:07:54** I had a discussion with a guy where I was discussing this exact example to the point
**00:07:54–00:07:59** that I was able to say that he was asking me how much running that we were doing in
**00:07:59–00:08:05** our AFL team at that time. And I said we actually did very little once we got to a high football
**00:08:05–00:08:12** component because we were able to manage football exposures. We were able to push up in speed.
**00:08:12–00:08:17** We were able to push up in contact drills. We were able to come down. We were able to
**00:08:17–00:08:25** manipulate that, quantify it. But all of that discipline built what our coach called nimble.
**00:08:25–00:08:30** So if he needed to make a change, he could come to me in a session and say, hey,
**00:08:30–00:08:34** I want to drop that last drill off. I want to stick with his second last drill. How long can
**00:08:34–00:08:39** I go for? And he knew and trusted that I would be able to make a calculation on our given rate,
**00:08:39–00:08:43** how we would be able to execute that in players that were available. I might say,
**00:08:43–00:08:48** hey, we can go for another 10 minutes here, but player A, B and C need to come out because
**00:08:49–00:08:54** they're at a position where they've just too much exposure because of wherever they're at.
**00:08:54–00:08:57** May have played more game time, et cetera. But my point in this is
**00:08:57–00:09:03** that the agility, the nimbleness that the coach wanted was derived from discipline.
**00:09:03–00:09:07** So when we look at this sort of stuff, when we say decision fatigue is real,
**00:09:07–00:09:11** big US interaction require micro decisions that deplete your willpower.
**00:09:11–00:09:16** I have worked with coaches where every interaction is ambiguous. What does that mean? What is this?
**00:09:16–00:09:25** What is that? It's just too hard. And this trains you. Now, you could argue where coaches
**00:09:25–00:09:30** didn't work well with me, did I not do enough? Maybe. The coaches that I just relayed that
**00:09:30–00:09:36** story about, clearly, I worked very hard early with him to establish a language and establish
**00:09:36–00:09:42** some technical guardrails, if you like. So we knew exactly what our drills were doing.
**00:09:42–00:09:48** The context switching. Now, apart from interrupting workflow states and the like,
**00:09:48–00:09:51** context switching, where you're going, we go back to the early example,
**00:09:52–00:09:58** how I worked with our training load, doctor to key coach to S&C. That is also draining,
**00:09:58–00:10:03** unless you've got control of that context. Now, we really want to coordinate this
**00:10:03–00:10:08** overhead because this fatigue is driven by coordination events. Now, when I started
**00:10:08–00:10:16** back in the late 90s in high performance sport, three people, Dr, physio, me, and then head coach,
**00:10:16–00:10:21** if you count that fall. But now, you're up within a 10-person team. You've got 45
**00:10:21–00:10:26** connection possibilities. When you're working with 20, it goes up. So you want to get this
**00:10:26–00:10:31** coordination piece down, Pat. Just not just communication, but as we've talked about in
**00:10:31–00:10:36** other areas, getting their people's jobs down, Pat, so they're very, very clear on what they're
**00:10:36–00:10:42** doing. So again, that military example, you're doing a tactical retreat. You know and trust
**00:10:42–00:10:48** that a staff member can get XYZ done, which again, allows you some space. But I would say,
**00:10:48–00:10:52** I do like this. The irony is that avoiding structure to stay flexible actually makes you
**00:10:52–00:10:58** reactive. That goes to my point in the first example. I had a coach who wanted to be nimble,
**00:10:58–00:11:04** but he became nimble by being the most disciplined coach I've ever worked with. And I can tell you,
